title: jaxcmr.experimental.serialreplagrank
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Calculations
    Participant summaries
    Contrasts
    Figures
    Transition tabulators
    API entries
    
    serialreplagrank
    tabulate_trial
    subject_serial_rep_lagrank
    test_first_second_bias
    plot_serial_rep_lagrank
    SerialRepLagRankTabulation
Proximity ranks for the first qualifying transition from a repeated item in serial recall.
On the study list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, an opening sequence A, B, X, H qualifies. X was reached in study order. The destination H lies close to the second presentation of X and far from the first. The rank for each presentation compares that distance with the distinct absolute lags to items still available from that presentation.
serialreplagrank returns scores by trial and presentation number. Once a transition qualifies, the remaining recalls on that trial contribute no ranks. The first recall initializes the run, and order checks begin with the second response. Select trials with a correct first recall if the run must begin at study position 1. A presentation with no rankable choice has an undefined score. subject_serial_rep_lagrank averages defined trial scores within participants.
This experimental analysis has a provisional interface and interpretation.

title: jaxcmr.experimental.prepared
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Prepared observations
    Likelihood reduction
    API entries
    
    PreparedPrediction
    PreparedLoss
    prediction_likelihood
Evaluate candidate parameters against observations prepared by a model.
For a model that predicts individual recall events, PreparedPrediction holds the observations, the function that predicts their probabilities, and masks identifying which events to score. prediction_likelihood combines those probabilities into one negative log likelihood per candidate. The model supplies probabilities conditioned on the full response history.
PreparedLoss pairs prepared observations with a function that directly scores a set of candidates. It can use the likelihood calculation above or a model-specific objective. Keeping observation arrays as arguments lets JAX reuse a compiled scoring function when the next participant’s data have compatible shapes and types.

jaxcmr.experimental.prepared.PreparedLoss(data, evaluate)

A population loss with explicit data and a stable evaluation function.
data must be a JAX-compatible pytree. evaluate accepts data, base parameters, free parameter names and a parameter matrix, returning one loss per column. Use a stable, pure function; observations belong in data, not in its closure. The function is static JIT metadata. Data leaves remain dynamic, so compatible shapes can share compilation across selections.
Preparation must snapshot mutable source data. Freezing this container prevents attribute reassignment but cannot freeze arbitrary Python objects supplied by a caller. JAX arrays and immutable containers are recommended. Use this object with the explicit experimental prepared fitters.

title: jaxcmr.experimental.set_permutation_likelihood
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Unordered recall
    API entries
    
    RecallSetLikelihoodLoss
    RecallPrefixLikelihoodLoss
Estimate the likelihood of recalling specified items in any order.
For observed items A and B, RecallSetLikelihoodLoss scores the event “A, B, STOP or B, A, STOP.” RecallPrefixLikelihoodLoss scores the event “the first two responses are A and B in either order.” Later responses are unrestricted in the prefix calculation. Repeated items retain their observed multiplicities.
Both losses sample orders uniformly and multiply the mean sequence probability by the number of distinct orders. This estimates the sum over orders without enumerating them all. The probability estimate is unbiased, though a finite sample can exceed one. Taking its logarithm introduces sampling bias into the fitted score.

title: jaxcmr.experimental.finite_window_race
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    First-passage probabilities
    CMR response policy
    API entries
    
    finite_window_probabilities
    FiniteWindowRace
Independent diffusion accumulators race to a common boundary at each recall.
A new unit-duration window starts at every retrieval attempt. STOP means that all eligible accumulators survived to the deadline. Each item gets the probability that its accumulator was the first to finish in that window.

FiniteWindowRace

jaxcmr.experimental.finite_window_race.FiniteWindowRace(list_length, parameters)

Use model evidence times race_drift_scale as drift toward race_boundary.
The boundary is positive. Time and diffusion noise are measured in units of one retrieval window. Neither a successful recall nor its probability is conditioned on some accumulator reaching the boundary.
Pass FiniteWindowRace as response_policy_create_fn to a compatible model factory. In ordinary CMR the drift for each item is race_drift_scale times the context-to-item memory output, before choice sensitivity or normalization.

title: jaxcmr.experimental.compound_cueing_crp
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Calculations
    Figures
    Transition tabulators
    API entries
    
    compound_cueing_crp
    tabulate_trial
    plot_compound_cueing
    CompoundCueingTabulation
Recall of a repeated item following two of its study neighbors.
Consider the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H. The recalls A then B form a pure cue for X because they occupied the two positions immediately before the same X, in that order. F then B form a mixed cue because F was two positions before the second X and B was one position before the first. In each case the next response determines whether X was recalled.
compound_cueing_crp pools opportunities and recalls separately for the two cue types and returns the pure and mixed probabilities in that order. A qualifying repeated item must still be available. Record its recall using its first study position for the actual count.
This experimental analysis has a provisional interface and interpretation.

title: jaxcmr.analyses.termination_probability
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Calculations
    Participant summaries
    Figures
    API entries
    
    conditional_termination_probability
    simple_termination_probability
    subject_output_length_mean
    subject_output_length_median
    plot_termination_probability
Where recall stops in the sequence of responses.
After studying A, B, C, a participant who recalls C, then A, then stops has an output length of two and a stop at output position 3. The first zero in the recorded sequence marks that stop. A sequence that fills every recorded slot also counts in the final bin, so that bin includes trials whose stopping time was never observed.
simple_termination_probability gives the fraction of all trials that stop at each position. conditional_termination_probability divides the same stop counts by the number of trials that reached each position. plot_termination_probability averages participant curves and shows the conditional probability by default. For a single length summary per participant, subject_output_length_mean and subject_output_length_median summarize the number of responses per trial.

Recall of each study item in its assigned output position.
For the study list A, B, C, D, a participant who recalls B, C and then stops receives no credit under strict serial scoring. B and C occurred in study order, but each came one response too early. In relative serial scoring, the transition from B to C earns credit for C.
trial_srac compares each response with the item studied at the corresponding position. If an item was presented twice, it can be correct in either of its assigned slots. srac averages the resulting indicators across trials, including trials with a blank at that position. plot_srac draws the mean of the participant curves.

Recall transitions between item conditions, adjusted for available targets.
The source is the item just recalled. The target is a candidate for the next recall. Suppose the source is a fruit and two vegetables are still available. Recalling either vegetable contributes one actual transition and two opportunities to the fruit-to-vegetable cell.
source_target_crp pools these counts across trials, then divides them cell by cell. Rows index source conditions and columns index target conditions. Cells with no available targets are undefined. Use subject_source_target_crp for a separate matrix per participant, or plot_source_target_crp to compare their mean probabilities.

Recall probability as a function of repeated-item spacing.
item_lag_counts counts one item’s opportunity and recall. Dataset operations pool these counts across lists; participant operations retain separate rows. Spacing is the number of intervening items between the first two presentations. Once-presented items occupy a separate leading column.
recall_probability_by_lag reports individual spacings with an overflow bucket at its configured maximum. binned_recall_probability_by_lag instead accepts explicit inclusive ranges and divides their pooled recalled-item counts by their pooled opportunities. It does not average per-spacing probabilities. Plots give each participant equal weight. Slope comparisons use explicit spacing coordinates and omit the once-presented column.

    RepRouteCRPTabulation
Where recall goes after reaching a repeated item from one of its neighbors.
In the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, consider the recalls B, X, H. B immediately preceded the first X at study, so it identifies the incoming route. H lies at lag +7 from the first X and +1 from the second. Both lags describe the same outgoing response. The route identifies the neighborhood of the incoming recall while leaving open which occurrence of X came to mind.
reproutecrp keeps the incoming neighborhood and the presentation used to measure outgoing lag as separate dimensions. The same-neighborhood curves measure lag from the incoming neighborhood’s X. The switch curves measure it from the other X. Compare those curves to see whether recalls cluster near one or the other presentation.

Transition lags grouped by proximity of the previous recall to a repeated item.
In the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, B lies one position before the first X. Transitions out of B therefore contribute to the row for cue offset −1 on the first-presentation surface. The columns give the lag of the next recall measured from B. For example, recalling C from B contributes at lag +2. Each cell divides actual transitions by opportunities at that offset and lag.
repcuecrp returns a surface per presentation. rep_cue_access selects the cells where the transition lands on the presentation itself. In the row for offset −1, this is lag +1. Selecting these cells across offsets gives the access curve. rep_cue_access_band summarizes that curve over a chosen range of offsets.

Recall transitions into an available repeated item.
In the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, suppose B has just been recalled and X is still available. B lies one position before the first X and seven before the second. This gives one opportunity at offset −1 on the first curve and one at −7 on the second. If X comes next, both receive an actual count at those offsets.
repaccesscrp pools actual counts and opportunities across trials. Its horizontal axis locates the previous recall relative to a presentation of the repeated item. repcrp answers the complementary question about the item recalled after X.

Study positions of the items recalled at a chosen output position.
Where on the study list did the second recall come from? Set query_recall_position=1 to get one value per study position for the second recall. On a trial with study list A, B, C and recalls C, A, the second recall credits study position 1. If A appeared more than once, it credits each of its study positions.
pnr divides the count at each study position by the total number of trials, including trials with no second recall. conditional_pnr_with_repeats uses a separate denominator for each position: the number of trials on which its item had yet to be recalled before the chosen output. An item can still count as available on a trial that ended early. plot_pnr averages these conditional curves across participants.

Temporal proximity of successive recalls relative to the choices still available.
After studying A, B, C, D and recalling B first, the available items A, C and D lie at absolute lags 1, 1 and 2. The default lagrank calculation ranks the two distinct lags. A transition to A or C scores 1, and a transition to D scores 0. Choosing an item uniformly in this example gives an expected score of 2/3.
With rank_method="item_midrank", each available item enters the ranking. A and C share the mean rank of their tied positions, so their scores are both 0.75 and D still scores 0. The expected score for uniform item choice is then 0.5. This method requires distinct study items. The default also handles repeated items by considering their possible study positions.
lagrank returns one mean score per trial. Transitions need a choice among at least two lag bins or two items, depending on the method. Trials without a scored transition return NaN. subject_lagrank averages the defined trial scores within each participant.
Use complete lists of the same length. When compiling lagrank, keep size and rank_method static.

Measurements associated with study items, and recall probability by measurement.
Use cat_factor_spc for measurement means at each study position, cat_factor_by_recall to separate those means by whether the item was recalled, and cat_recall_by_factor for recall probability within measurement bins. Fields and category values are explicit inputs; the operations do not assume a particular experiment or measurement unit.
Dataset calculations pool eligible presentations. Their subject_* counterparts keep participants separate, and plotters average participant summaries with equal weight. Missing measurements and optional quality flags exclude observations, while recall status credits every occurrence of a recalled item. Shared bins keep dataset comparisons on the same scale.

cat_factor_spc

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.cat_factor_spc(dataset, category_field, category_value, factor_field, *, valid_field=None)

Return mean measurements by study position within one category.
A “factor” is a numeric measurement attached to each presentation, such as LPP amplitude. factor_field and category_field name arrays shaped (trials, study_positions), aligned with pres_itemnos. Recalls are not used.
At each position, average finite measurements from the selected category across trials. Exclude padding, presentations after the declared event count, and any nonfinite or nonpositive flags in the optional valid_field. Return one value per study position; positions with no eligible measurements are NaN.
This pools observations. Use subject_cat_factor_spc for separate participant means and its plotting wrapper for equal-participant weighting. JIT requires field names static; the category value may vary dynamically.


cat_factor_by_recall

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.cat_factor_by_recall(dataset, category_field, category_value, factor_field, *, valid_field=None)

Return measurement means with axes (recall_status, study_position).
factor_field selects a numeric measurement per presentation, such as LPP amplitude; it and category_field align with pres_itemnos. Rows are [recalled, not recalled], with means pooled across eligible trials.
All eligible presentations of a recalled item enter the recalled group. A response position identifies the item, not which occurrence was remembered. Duplicate responses count once; invalid codes and padding add no hits.
Within each category/status/position group, average finite measurements at actual presentations. Optional valid_field flags must be finite and positive. Missing measurements and quality failures exclude observations from means without changing whether the item was recalled. Empty groups are NaN. Use subject_cat_factor_by_recall for separate participant means rather than pooling trials.
Field names must be static under JIT.


compute_factor_bin_edges

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.compute_factor_bin_edges(values, valid, bin_count=10)

Return equal-width edges from finite, included reference values.
valid must match values. No eligible values gives all-NaN edges. Constant values get a symmetric interval with half-width max(0.5, abs(value) * 0.01) so the edges remain distinct at large scales. This helper supports JIT with a positive, static integer bin_count. It does not inspect recall outcomes or infer which datasets/categories should define the bins.


binned_recall_counts

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.binned_recall_counts(recalled, values, include, bin_edges)

Return recalled and eligible counts for fixed bins, in that order.
Inputs share a shape, with one Boolean recall indicator per observation. Missing/nonfinite and out-of-range values contribute to neither count. Bins are left-closed/right-open, except the final bin includes its right edge. Empty bins have zero counts; rates derived from them are undefined.
Supply a one-dimensional array of at least two finite, strictly increasing edges. Numerical calls assume aligned inputs and valid edges. All-NaN edges from an empty reference set yield zero counts.


category_factor_recall_histogram

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.category_factor_recall_histogram(recalls, factor, categories, category_value, bin_edges, *, valid=None)

Pool recalled-position indicators within a category and fixed bins.
This array interface identifies recalled positions directly; it has no item identities with which to expand repeated presentations. Use the dataset operation cat_recall_by_factor for repeated-item experiments.
Repeated responses count once; zero, negative and out-of-range recall codes do not mark any position. valid excludes unusable study positions from both numerator and denominator. Empty bins return NaN, never zero.


cat_recall_by_factor

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.cat_recall_by_factor(dataset, category_field, category_value, factor_field, bin_edges=None, bin_count=10, *, valid_field=None)

Return recall probabilities within bins of a presentation measurement.
A “factor” is a numeric measurement per presentation, such as LPP amplitude. factor_field and category_field select trial-by-study-position arrays aligned with pres_itemnos. The output has one recall probability per bin, not a mean measurement as in cat_factor_by_recall.
For the chosen category, divide recalled-position counts by eligible-position counts in each bin. Recall codes name study positions; duplicate responses count once. All eligible presentations of a recalled item contribute to recall counts. Exclude padding, presentations after the declared event count, nonfinite measurements, and values outside the bins from both counts. Optional valid_field flags must be finite and positive. Empty bins return NaN. Bins include their left edge; only the final bin also includes its right edge.
Automatic edges use finite, eligible measurements across all categories in this dataset. For comparisons, compute reference edges once with compute_factor_bin_edges and pass them to each call. This function pools positions; subject_cat_recall_by_factor returns participant rates that can be averaged with equal participant weight in each available bin.
JIT requires field names and bin_count static. The category and explicit bin-edge values may vary dynamically at a fixed shape.


subject_cat_factor_spc

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.subject_cat_factor_spc(dataset, trial_mask, category_field, category_values, factor_field, *, valid_field=None)

Return separate subject means, sorted by ID and in requested category order.
Subjects without selected trials are omitted. Empty selections return a zero-length subject axis. Averaging this axis with jnp.nanmean gives equal weight to subjects with data in each cell. Grouping runs outside JIT; the within-subject calculation is compiled.


subject_cat_factor_by_recall

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.subject_cat_factor_by_recall(dataset, trial_mask, category_field, category_values, factor_field, *, valid_field=None)

Return subject-by-category-by-status-by-position factor means.
Subject IDs are sorted; category order follows the caller; statuses are [recalled, not recalled]. Subjects without selected trials are omitted. Empty selections return a zero-length subject axis. Grouping runs outside JIT; each subject calculation is compiled. Averaging the subject axis with jnp.nanmean weights available subjects equally in each cell.


subject_cat_recall_by_factor

jaxcmr.analyses.factors.subject_cat_recall_by_factor(dataset, trial_mask, category_field, category_values, factor_field, bin_edges, *, valid_field=None)

Return subject rates using caller-supplied common edges.
Subjects occur in ascending ID order, omitting those without selected trials. Category order follows category_values. An empty selection returns shape (0, n_categories, n_bins). Each subject pools its own eligible positions; jnp.nanmean(result, axis=0) then weights subjects equally within each available bin. This grouping wrapper runs outside JIT; each subject’s numerical calculation is compiled.

Conditional response probability by distance between recalled items.
Given the previous recall, which distances were available for the next recall, and which distance did the participant choose? tabulate_trial uses the items’ global identifiers in pres_itemids to look up distances in a vocabulary matrix. A transition contributes one opportunity to every bin containing an available item, even if several items share a bin. The chosen item’s bin also receives one actual transition.
dist_crp pools these counts across trials and divides within each bin. Use common bin edges when comparing curves. Edges can come from percentiles of the matrix or from distances to available items on selected trials. For the latter, the target bin count is the requested minimum multiplied by the number of participants. Counts are pooled, so participants can contribute unequally and the final bin can fall short.

    crp

    SimpleTabulation
    Tabulation
Conditional response probability by lag between successive recalls.
Suppose a participant studies A, B, C, D and recalls B followed by C. That transition has lag +1 because C was studied one position after B. From B, the participant could also have recalled A (lag −1) or D (lag +2). The trial therefore contributes one actual transition at +1 and one opportunity at each of −1, +1 and +2.
tabulate_trial counts actual and available lags. crp sums both across trials and divides at each lag. A lag with no opportunities has an undefined probability. plot_crp calculates probabilities per participant before averaging them.
For a list with repeated items, one recall refers to all presentations of its item. A transition can then contribute at several lags. Each distinct lag counts at most once per transition in each tally. For lists of distinct items, simple_crp needs only the position-coded recalls and list length.
Use complete study lists of the same length in a call. The numerical calculations can be JIT-compiled with a fixed list width and occurrence capacity (size).

    DistanceTabulation
Distance-binned transition probabilities for selected recall events.
For recalls A, B, C, selecting only the transition into C measures the distance from B to C. The earlier recall of A still removes A from the alternatives available after B. Use this calculation to restrict which events contribute while retaining the participant’s recall history.
dist_crp reads the event mask from _should_tabulate and looks up distances using global item identifiers. At each selected transition it counts the bin of the chosen item and the bins that contained at least one available item. It pools those counts across trials. plot_dist_crp accepts event masks alongside the trial selections and uses common bins to compare participant curves.

Recall probability by study position within a category.
For each study position, cat_spc asks how often the item was recalled on trials where an item of the specified category occupied that position. Suppose a fruit appeared first on two lists and third on eight. The two points on the fruit curve have denominators of two and eight respectively. A position with no eligible fruit has an undefined probability.
The dataset supplies the category at each presentation. Recalling an item credits each eligible presentation of it once. plot_cat_spc averages the participant curves. To pool eligible presentations across positions into one rate per category, use cat_recall_rate.

Estimate model parameters from a loss evaluated on selected trials.
The loss determines what counts as a good fit. For example, a likelihood loss scores the observed recall sequence, while an SPC loss compares observed and simulated serial position curves. The fitter searches within the free-parameter bounds for values that minimize the chosen loss.
ScipyDE and the Evosax differential-evolution fitters compare populations of candidates. ScipyLBFGSB and ScipyTrustConstr use loss gradients and can search from several starting points. ParameterSpace translates between search coordinates and physical parameter values. Results report parameters in the units used by the model.
A pooled fit estimates one parameter set from all selected trials. Participant-wise fitting estimates a set for each participant. In a FitResult, each row links a parameter set to its objective value and optimizer results. parameters_for_subjects uses those rows to assign a pooled estimate or matching participant estimates for simulation.

ScipyLBFGSB

jaxcmr.fitting.ScipyLBFGSB(dataset, features, base_params, model_factory_cls, loss_fn_cls, hyperparams=None)

Fit a differentiable loss with box bounds and reproducible restarts.
The constructor accepts the same dataset, model factory and loss factory as the DE fitters, including configured callable loss constructors. Optimization uses explicit unit-interval coordinates for parameter scaling; the loss always receives physical parameter values. SciPy owns the local optimizer. Only loss evaluation and differentiation use JAX.
Required hyperparameter: bounds (a nonempty name -> [lower, upper] mapping of finite, strictly ordered bounds). Optional controls: transforms (a name -> ‘linear’/‘log’/‘log1p’/‘exp_neg’ mapping), sampling_transforms (same syntax, defaults to transforms), initial_params (one complete physical starting mapping, refined first), best_of (maximum local solves, default 8), screening_size (64), screening_batch_size (16), min_start_distance (0.1), seed (0), num_steps (500), max_fun (15000), relative_tolerance (1e-9), gradient_tolerance (1e-5), max_line_search_steps (30), time_limit_seconds (None), and local_time_limit_seconds (None, an allowance for each restart). These defaults describe L-BFGS-B; the trust-constr subclass documents its solver-specific controls. By default, score a Latin-hypercube bank and refine promising, separated candidates. Distances are RMS differences in those sampling coordinates; optimization uses transforms independently. Set screening_size=0 for unscreened uniform restarts; combine this with best_of=1 and initial_params for local polishing. Transforms are explicit: CMR can use {‘primacy_decay’: ‘exp_neg’} to fit retention while preserving its physical decay parameter and bounds.
Time limits include screening and all restarts and are checked between evaluations. One initial value/gradient is always allowed as a fallback, recorded explicitly if late. Later improvements are retained only when evaluated before both deadlines; in-flight work cannot be interrupted. Call warmup(mask) to measure compilation separately. Without warmup, compilation counts toward the time limits. Nonfinite values/gradients end that restart, with diagnostics retained; a finite objective with an invalid gradient is never reported as a good fit.
Uses the caller’s JAX precision configuration; it never changes global JAX settings. Double precision is recommended for tight tolerances and bounds near singular model limits. The loss must supply meaningful derivatives; differentiability cannot be inferred from the general LossFn protocol.
Caller requirements: counts are positive integers, except screening_size may be zero. min_start_distance lies in [0, 1]; tolerances are finite and nonnegative; supplied time limits, trust radii and barrier parameters are finite and positive. initial_params must name every free parameter once with finite values inside its bounds. L-BFGS-B-only options must not be passed to trust-constr.

jaxcmr.fitting.ScipyTrustConstr(dataset, features, base_params, model_factory_cls, loss_fn_cls, hyperparams=None)

Bounded trust-constr with JAX gradients and SciPy’s BFGS curvature.
Accepts the same dataset, model, loss and FitResult contract as ScipyLBFGSB. Required option: bounds. Shared controls include transforms, sampling_transforms, initial_params, screening, seed, restart count, and global/per-restart time limits. Sampling defaults to the optimization coordinates; use an explicit mapping to choose a different distribution.
Defaults: best_of=4, screening_size=64, screening_batch_size=16, min_start_distance=0.1, num_steps=1000, gradient_tolerance=1e-7, step_tolerance=1e-12, barrier_tolerance=1e-10, initial_trust_radius=1.0, initial_barrier_parameter=0.1. L-BFGS-B’s max_fun, relative_tolerance and max_line_search_steps controls are not accepted. No Hessian is differentiated or compiled: SciPy updates its curvature estimate from the gradients.
Call warmup(mask) before imposing short fitting budgets. Deadlines include screening and restarts and are checked between evaluations. One initial evaluation is guaranteed as a fallback; any late fallback is identified in diagnostics. Successful solver termination is not proof of a global optimum.

jaxcmr.fitting.ParameterSpace(bounds, transforms=None)

Map bounded model parameters to unit-interval optimization coordinates.
bounds and all model-facing values use physical parameter units. Selected parameters may use log, log1p, or exp(-decay) coordinates before their transformed interval is scaled to [0, 1]. This changes the geometry of optimization and uniform sampling, not the model family.

The probability of stopping depends on which candidates remain available. A model can stop only on exhaustion, use a schedule indexed by recall count, or compare support for available and unavailable studied candidates. Each calculation returns one if retrieval has ended or no candidates remain.
A model with a fixed stopping rule can call the corresponding function directly. Configurable CMR variants use these calculations through the response policy that assigns probabilities to STOP and each item.

    Which models support each rule?
A response distribution gives the probability of STOP followed by each item.
In ordinary CMR the model weights each item by its context match. A semantic model can add the last recalled item’s semantic associations. A positional model can sum the weights of several study positions for the same item. PositionalStop and RecallUntilExhausted use the weights supplied by the model.
Other rules compete STOP directly against raw evidence. They require a model that supplies evidence in those units. LearnedStopCompetition also requires the model to encode a terminal item during study.

from jaxcmr.components.response import PowerLawStopCompetition
from jaxcmr.components.support_ratio import RawSupportRatioSoftmaxChoice
from jaxcmr.models import cmr, terminal_item_cmr

ratio_factory = cmr.make_factory(response_policy_create_fn=RawSupportRatioSoftmaxChoice)
competition_factory = cmr.make_factory(response_policy_create_fn=PowerLawStopCompetition)
terminal_factory = terminal_item_cmr.make_factory()

title: jaxcmr.components.response
text:
Which models support each rule?



Response rule
Models that supply its inputs




Scheduled stopping or recall until exhaustion
All configurable CMR variants. Semantic and emotional models provide their own item weights. Positional models sum weights over occurrences of each item.


Raw support-ratio policies, exponential or power-law STOP competition, exponential-evidence support ratio, or the finite-window race
Ordinary CMR, CMR without reinstatement, outlist CMR, eCMR (including additive semantic and source-switch eCMR), CMR3 and its source-switch variant, and terminal-item CMR expose raw evidence. The additive semantic retrieval-bias variant requires a policy using candidate weights because its bias operates after the choice transform. Blended positional CMR supplies evidence separately for each route.


Competition with a learned terminal item
Terminal-item CMR encodes an end-of-list item and supplies its evidence alongside the study items.



Historical fits can select RelativePowerSupportRatio. It computes candidate weights separately for available and unavailable items, then divides their totals. Use that policy to reproduce fits made with separately weighted groups.
Dual-cue CMR stops when it exhausts its candidates and has a fixed response rule.

Instance memory stores each association as a separate trace. A retrieval cue gives each trace a weight based on its match to the stored input. The response is the sum of the stored outputs multiplied by those weights.
probe scales the strongest positive match to one and raises each relative match to the trace sensitivity. probe_without_scale uses the raw matches, giving the same result as a linear memory built from those traces.

Temporal context is the cue a CMR model uses to retrieve items. At the start of a list, only the start-of-list unit is active. Studying or recalling an item can move context toward the pattern associated with that item.
Use context.init when the model supplies only start-of-list and item cues. TemporalContext.init_expanded also reserves one fresh unit per item. Outlist CMR uses a fresh unit when it studies an item again. Source-switch models use one when a change of source triggers drift. Each call to integrate_with_outlist consumes one of these units.

A terminal-item CMR trial learns an association for the end of the list.
For a study list [A, B, C], the associative memories represent [A, B, C, END]. At the end of study the model associates END with the current context. During retrieval the default response policy uses the evidence for END to score STOP. The recorded outcomes are STOP (0) and the three study-item codes (1–3).

Each model module supplies a make_factory function. It binds the component creators and returns a factory class. Construct that class with the dataset and any vocabulary features or similarities. Its create_trial_model method takes a trial index and a parameter mapping.
The semantic factories prepare a connection matrix for each trial. The emotional-source factories prepare a category for each local item. Both use the selected trial’s item codes when constructing its model. Each configurable factory takes a response policy that assigns probabilities to STOP and each item. The positional and blended models account for repeated presentations before returning a probability for the recorded item.

    sequence_probabilities

    mask_trailing_terminations
    mask_first_recall_and_terminations
Score the observed order of recall under a memory-search model.
If a participant recalls C and then A, the model assigns a probability to C after study and a probability to A after retrieving C. sequence_probabilities follows those same responses through a model that is ready to retrieve. MemorySearchLikelihoodLoss first presents each trial’s study list and translates recorded study positions into the model’s item codes. It then sums the negative log probabilities of the selected events across trials.
Use the named losses to omit the first response, termination, or both from the score. Omitting C from the score in this example still conditions the probability of A on C. A recorded zero represents STOP. Omitting its contribution leaves the model’s stopping rule active when it assigns probabilities to items.

Copy supplied example inputs into a project.

Construct and transform recall datasets while keeping trial fields aligned.
make_dataset builds a dataset from recall sequences and study information. select_trials selects, reorders or repeats whole trial rows, carrying participant IDs, study lists and custom fields along with the responses. replace_recalls supplies new responses and removes metadata tied to the old recall events.
A recorded response identifies a one-based study position. Models use the identity of the item presented there. For the study list A, B, A, a response at position 3 becomes A under recall_positions_to_items. Converting A back with recall_items_to_positions gives position 1, its first occurrence.
Use select_conditions to inspect which trials and participants meet a selection, and select_trials to take those rows. apply_by_subject groups selected trials by participant and calls an analysis on each group. Condition inspection and participant grouping run on the host. Array-based selection and recall replacement support JAX transformations with fixed output shapes.

    negative_log_likelihood
Numerical operations for memory-search models and likelihood calculations.
Use relative_power_scale to sharpen or flatten nonnegative support while keeping its largest positive value at one. The caller determines what the support represents and how the resulting weights enter the model.
normalize_magnitude converts nonzero vectors to unit length. cosine_similarity_matrix applies that normalization to each row of an item-feature matrix, then returns pairwise dot products.
exponential_primacy_decay assigns weights to zero-based study positions, with an exponential primacy effect above a baseline of one. negative_log_likelihood sums negative log probabilities over supplied events; the caller chooses which events contribute.
These operations take numerical values or arrays directly, so they can be used within model calculations or independently of a model.
FLOAT32_EPS is float32 machine epsilon, exactly 2**-23. Its value stays fixed when used in float64 calculations.

jaxcmr.math.relative_power_scale(value, scale)

Default

Finite, nonnegative support. The maximum is taken over the entire array; use jax.vmap to transform several vectors independently.

floating array
Same shape as value. Positive entries equal (value / max(value)) ** scale, including at scale one. Zero entries remain zero, and all-zero input returns zeros.

Summarize fitted parameters and compare models using their scores.
Use the numerical functions, such as aic_scores, when you have arrays of scores and want to work with the results directly. When you have named model records, the comparison functions align rows by participant ID and produce labelled tables. Which observations were fitted and what a score measures must agree across the models in a comparison.
summarize_parameters describes the distribution of parameter estimates across fitted rows. For comparing models, information criteria start with summed negative log likelihoods and penalize the number of free parameters. Paired differences and win fractions describe how the models compare for the same participants. Held-out comparisons use the supplied test scores. For declared nested models, floor_nested_fitness makes a reporting adjustment and records which scores it changed.
To estimate model frequencies in a population, random_effects_model_selection takes one row of log evidences per participant, with one column per model. bayesian_model_selection prepares that comparison from fitted likelihoods using an information-criterion approximation. A single fit to pooled observations supplies only one estimate, regardless of the number of participants who contributed trials.

On this page
  
    
    
    Preparing a plot
    Drawing summaries

    Arranging comparisons

    API entries
    
    init_plot
    prepare_plot_inputs

    bootstrap_mean_errors
    format_analysis_axes
    matrix_heatmap
    comparison_panels
    iter_condition_curves
    iter_analysis_figures
    save_figure
Draw behavioral summaries and arrange comparisons across datasets and conditions.
If you have a recall dataset, start with the plotter for the measure you want, such as jaxcmr.analyses.spc.plot_spc. It selects trials, calculates a serial position curve for each participant, and passes those curves to plot_mean_curve. If you already have participant scores, you can call plot_mean_curve directly. Each row is an observation and each column a position or bin. The mean and optional bootstrap interval therefore give each participant with a finite score equal weight in that column.
When writing an analysis plotter, use prepare_plot_inputs to obtain axes, trial selections and colors. Several mean curves can share those axes. format_analysis_axes labels them after the curves are drawn. For a matrix of values, matrix_heatmap displays the cells on a common color scale.
comparison_panels arranges datasets and trial selections before an analysis runs. iter_condition_curves works with participant scores that have already been calculated, separating them into curves for individual conditions. To run several configured analyses, iter_analysis_figures calls their plotters and yields each figure for display or saving.

title: Contributing to JAXCMR
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Set up a checkout
    Change and test the library
    Edit notebooks and documentation
    
    Change a notebook
    Change an API reference entry
    Change an input supplied with the package
    Preview and share your change
The Python source lives in jaxcmr/ and the tests in tests/. If you’re editing something readers see on the website, your starting point might be a Python docstring, a guide page, or a template notebook.

title: Contributing to JAXCMR
text:
Set up a checkout
A checkout is your local copy of the repository. Open a terminal in its top-level folder, the one containing pyproject.toml and uv.lock. If you still need a copy, follow the checkout instructions. Run the commands on this page from that folder.
uv sync --locked --extra test --group reader --group docs
uv sync prepares a Python environment in .venv and installs JAXCMR from your checkout. The next time you start Python in that environment, it uses your edited source. Syncing can remove packages outside the selection from an existing environment.

--locked uses the package versions recorded in uv.lock. If the lockfile needs updating, uv stops and tells you.
--extra test includes pytest, the program that runs the library tests.
--group reader adds tools for running and checking notebooks.
--group docs adds the Python tools for generating the API reference. To render web pages, also install Quarto 1.11.9.

title: Contributing to JAXCMR
text:
Change and test the library
The serial position curve answers a question about each study position. What fraction of the items presented there were recalled? The calculation is spc in jaxcmr/analyses/spc.py. Its tests are in tests/test_recall_measures.py. Run them once before editing so you know which checks already pass.
uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/test_recall_measures.py
uv run --no-sync uses the environment you just prepared and skips the installation step. python -m pytest starts pytest with that environment’s Python. The path selects one test file. At the end, pytest reports how many tests passed or failed. For a failure, it shows the test name and the comparison that failed.
Give your change a test whose expected result you can work out by hand. Suppose the study lists are [A, B, A] and [C, D]. The participant recalls A twice on the first trial and nothing on the second. Each position where A was studied gets credit once. The recall fractions for positions 1, 2, and 3 are 1/2, 0/2, and 1/1. Only the first list contributes to the third denominator. In the test file, look for test_position_codes_recall_all_presentations_without_double_counting to see how a similar list and its expected scores are written in Python. Run the same test command after editing the function and its test.
If you change how the experimental CMR fitters prepare observations, run uv run --no-sync python -m pytest -m audit. Here -m audit selects the tests that check whether JAX can reuse a compiled calculation when the selected trials change.

title: Contributing to JAXCMR
text:
Edit notebooks and documentation

Change a notebook
To change the category recall rate template, open templates/cat_recall_rate.ipynb. Tutorial and Library Guide notebooks live in guide/tutorials/ and guide/overview/. If you change a calculation, select the checkout’s Python environment as the notebook kernel, run the cells, and save the output you want readers to see. For a text-only edit, the existing output can stay.
You can then test the saved template from the terminal.
uv run --no-sync python guide/tools/check_notebooks.py --select cat_recall_rate
The script runs a temporary copy with a small workload and checks its results. Your original keeps the settings and output you saved. The script prints the path to a report showing which notebooks passed. --select picks one notebook by its name, such as cat_recall_rate. Omit it to run the whole collection.


Change an API reference entry
Suppose you’re clarifying the entry for simulate_dataset. Edit the description inside that function in jaxcmr/simulation.py (its docstring). The docstring at the top of the module supplies the page introduction. To add an entry or move it under a different heading, edit the list in guide/reference/_simulation.yml.
quarto render guide/reference/simulation.qmd
This rebuilds the simulation reference page. In the local website preview, open API Reference → Memory models → Simulation and follow the function’s link in the summary table.


Change an input supplied with the package
If a notebook uses one of JAXCMR’s bundled datasets or saved fits, edit the source file under data/. For a new file, also add its path to _EXAMPLE_FILES in jaxcmr/examples.py, so copy_example_inputs recognizes it, and to the wheel and source-archive file lists in pyproject.toml, so it ships with the package.
Add --reinstall-package jaxcmr to the setup command above to refresh the installed copy of the data. Rerun the notebook that reads it. To check that someone installing the package also receives the file, run uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/test_distribution.py. These tests build and install the package in a fresh environment and need internet access for dependencies.


Preview and share your change
The website’s theme, navigation, and default code controls are set in guide/_quarto.yml. Edit guide/styles.scss for layout shared by light and dark mode. The palette files supply colors. Command-oriented pages use guide/_commands.yml to show commands without line numbers. Formatting specific to API entries lives in guide/reference/reference.css.
The API sidebar also supplies the group names and links for the homepage and reference index. Edit the page descriptions in guide/reference/index.qmd.
Published notebooks carry a copy of their code controls so readers can render a download on its own. After changing those defaults, run uv run --no-sync python guide/prepare.py --sync-notebook-format to refresh those settings in the notebook sources.
After changing shared styling or navigation, build the whole site. Quarto embeds the sidebar in each page, so a single-page render updates only one copy.
bash build-docs.sh
uv run --no-sync python guide/tools/check_site.py docs
uv run --no-sync python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory docs
The first command builds the site in docs/ using the outputs already saved in the notebooks. The second checks local links, notebook downloads, and example files. The third serves the built pages at http://127.0.0.1:8000/, where the browser can load Quarto’s navigation scripts. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the server. To inspect a revised notebook, use its download link. Open in Colab opens the version on GitHub’s main branch.
To propose a code or documentation change, open a pull request asking to merge the edits on your branch into JAXCMR. If you’re working in your own copy on GitHub, follow GitHub’s instructions for submitting from a fork. Describe what will change for readers or researchers and how you checked it. GitHub runs the routine library tests on Linux, macOS, and Windows and checks the website build. The notebook runner and the clean-install tests run locally, so include their results if you ran them.

text:
On this page

A serial position curve shows how often participants recall an item as a function of its position on the study list. A recall at any output position counts.

title: Serial position curves
text:
Configure this run
Choose response files, condition queries and an output folder. The default complete_lists_only=True restricts curves to lists with no padded study slots. A recalled item credits all of its eligible study positions, once per trial; there is no occurrence-capacity setting.
Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.


1 — Set the parameters for this run
# Inputs and saved results — change these for your project.
project_root = None  # Explicit folder, enclosing Git root, or current directory.
data_path = None  # A supplied single path takes precedence over data_paths.
data_paths = [
    "data/Dupertuys2026.h5",
    "data/simulations/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo_best_of_3.h5",
    "data/simulations/Dupertuys2026_eCMR_source_only_demo_best_of_3.h5",

]

# Observation selection — queries use fields in your dataset.

    "jnp.equal(data['list_type'], 2)",

text:
Prepare the environment and inputs
Run the following setup cells once, then continue in order. The short installation cell runs only in Colab; local and Slurm runs use the environment you selected during Setup.
project_root anchors relative paths. When it is unset, Colab uses the current directory; elsewhere the notebook uses the enclosing Git project if present, or the current directory. Custom input paths remain your responsibility.

3 — Import packages
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from jaxcmr.analyses.spc import plot_spc
from jaxcmr.dataset import select_conditions
from jaxcmr.examples import copy_example_inputs
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data
from jaxcmr.helpers import resolve_project_path, resolve_project_root
from jaxcmr.plotting import save_figure

title: Serial position curves
text:
Select the observations
select_conditions returns the masks and participant coverage without altering your data. Check the printed list and participant counts before interpreting the results. Queries are Python expressions evaluated with the dataset named data; replace the supplied condition codes with those in your data. trial_query overrides the list of trial_queries and uses selection_label.
With data_path set, the notebook reads that file and compares conditions. With data_path=None, data_paths and data_labels produce one panel per condition comparing datasets—even if the list contains just one file. Labels must correspond to the supplied selections and files.


4 — Resolve input paths, conditions and output settings
root_path = resolve_project_root(project_root)
print("Project directory:", root_path)

copy_example_inputs([data_path] if data_path is not None else data_paths, base_dir=root_path)

output_dir = resolve_project_path(output_dir, root_path)
figure_dir = (
    resolve_project_path(figure_dir, root_path)
    if figure_dir is not None
    else output_dir
)

queries = trial_queries if trial_query is None else [trial_query]
condition_labels = labels if trial_query is None else [selection_label]
input_paths = [data_path] if data_path is not None else data_paths
input_paths = [resolve_project_path(path, root_path) for path in input_paths]
input_labels = [selection_label] if data_path is not None else data_labels
if len(queries) != len(condition_labels) or len(input_paths) != len(input_labels):
    raise ValueError("Supply a label for each input and each condition query.")




5 — Load the supplied response datasets
datasets = [load_data(str(path), max_subjects=max_subjects) for path in input_paths]




6 — Select observations and report participant counts
selected_conditions = [
    select_conditions(dataset, queries, complete_lists_only=complete_lists_only)
    for dataset in datasets
]
masks_by_dataset = [[condition.mask for condition in group] for group in selected_conditions]
for dataset_label, group in zip(input_labels, selected_conditions):
    for condition_label, condition in zip(condition_labels, group):
        print(
            f"{dataset_label} / {condition_label}: {condition.trial_count} lists, "
            f"{condition.participant_count} participants"
        )
data, trial_masks = datasets[0], masks_by_dataset[0]

title: Serial position curves
text:
Calculate and interpret the curves
The analysis calculates recall by study position within each participant, then displays participant means and bootstrap confidence intervals. For repeated study identities, recalling the item credits each eligible presentation position once per trial.
Compare the shape and magnitude of curves under matched observation selections. Confidence intervals describe uncertainty across participants; they do not by themselves test a difference between curves. Use separate statistical comparisons for a specific hypothesis.


7 — Prepare the condition and dataset comparison panels
panels = comparison_panels(
    datasets, masks_by_dataset, input_labels, condition_labels,
    mode="conditions" if data_path is not None else "datasets",
    selection_label=selection_label,
)




8 — Calculate, plot and save the selected comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(panels), 1, figsize=(8, 3.8 * len(panels)), squeeze=False)
for ax, panel in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
    panel_data = panel["datasets"]
    panel_masks = panel["trial_masks"]
    curve_labels = panel["labels"]
    title = panel["title"]
    plot_spc(
        panel_data,
        panel_masks,
        labels=curve_labels,
        contrast_name=contrast_name,
        color_cycle=color_cycle,
        confidence_level=confidence_level,
        axis=ax,
        bootstrap_seed=plot_seed,
    )
    ax.set_title(title)

    if ax.get_legend_handles_labels()[1]:
        ax.legend(title=contrast_name)
    if ylim is not None:
        ax.set_ylim(ylim[0], ylim[1])
    if yticks is not None:
        ax.set_yticks(yticks)
if figure_str:
    save_figure(str(figure_dir), figure_str, figure=plt.gcf())
else:
    plt.gcf().tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
On this page

    Reuse the results
Use this procedure to ask which study positions supply the first, third, or another response in a recall sequence. It reads observed or simulated responses and saves curves for the output positions and conditions you select.
Study position describes where an item appeared during presentation; output position describes when it was recalled. This distinction matters when configuring and interpreting later-recall curves.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Recall by output position
text:
Configure this run
Choose response files and conditions, then set output_positions. These are zero-based: [0, 2] means the first and third response. The optional query_recall_position overrides that list with a single position. Requested positions must fit within the stored recall array.
The default selects complete study lists. size controls the capacity for repeated study identities, as in the serial-position analysis.
Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.

text:
Interpret the output-position curves
The plot divides actual choices at each study position by opportunities where that item remains available at the selected output position, within participant. At the first output this describes first-recall probability; later outputs condition on availability after prior recalls. Later curves need not sum to one across study positions.
A zero-padded missing response contributes no actual choice. The calculation is not restricted to sequences that produced a response at that output position. The figure then averages participant curves and shows participant-bootstrap intervals.

title: Comparing pooled model fits
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Configure this run
    Prepare the environment and inputs
    Establish a comparable set of fits
    Recalculate likelihoods
    Compare fit scores and search histories
    Compare saved predictions
    Reuse the results
Use this procedure to compare saved pooled model fits and their saved predictions. It checks the observations and objective conventions, recalculates likelihoods, and saves a model-comparison table alongside optimization histories and behavioral figures.
You need at least two compatible pooled fit records, their response files and response provenance. Fitting and simulation are separate procedures. The results here concern parameter sets fitted across participants; they are not a comparison of independent participant estimates.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Comparing pooled model fits
text:
Configure this run
Use matching model keys in fit_paths, simulation_paths and model_labels. Supply the same observations used for fitting. The shared fit selection is read from the records; the behavioral display selection is configured separately through analysis_trial_query or individual analysis configurations.
Choose output_dir for the comparison table and figures. The behavioral analysis list selects what to inspect; a better fit score does not guarantee better predictions for every behavioral measure.
Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.


1 — Configure the saved fits and response files
# Inputs and saved results — change these for your project.
project_root = None  # Explicit folder, enclosing Git root, or current directory.
data_path = "data/Dupertuys2026.h5"
output_dir = "results/model_comparison"

# Models and saved fits — names connect specifications, labels and outputs.
fit_paths = {
    "CMR": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo.json",
    "eCMR_source_only": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_eCMR_source_only.json",
    "eCMR_broad": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_eCMR_broad.json",
}
simulation_paths = {

Feature composition stays explicit here. feature_column selects the categorical feature, and concat_features=True combines categorical columns before semantic columns. When concatenation is requested, supply both feature arrays; otherwise the configured concatenation fails rather than substituting a different feature set.


4 — Define feature loading and model construction
def load_features(spec):
    if spec.get("concat_features", False):
        semantic = np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["embedding_path"], root_path))
        categorical = np.load(
            resolve_project_path(spec["emotion_feature_path"], root_path)
        )[:, int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) : int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) + 1]
        return np.concatenate([categorical, semantic], axis=1)
    semantic = np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["embedding_path"], root_path)) if spec.get("embedding_path") else None
    categorical = (
        np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["emotion_feature_path"], root_path))[
            :,
            int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) : int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) + 1,
        ]
        if spec.get("emotion_feature_path")
        else None
    )
    return categorical if categorical is not None else semantic


def construct_model(spec):
    return model_factory_from_paths(spec["model_factory"], spec["components"])

title: Comparing pooled model fits
section: Establish a comparable set of fits
text:
Establish a comparable set of fits
All records must contain one pooled fit and the same nonempty set of observation rows. The notebook also checks the recorded input path when available, objective and stopping policy. A matching path does not establish identical data: use the same observations for every fit, and refit after changing them. Models may differ in mechanisms and free parameters, but their likelihood scores must refer to comparable observations and conventions.


6 — Load the named pooled fits
records = {name: json.loads(resolve_project_path(path, root_path).read_text()) for name, path in fit_paths.items()}
# The bundled records predate the move of this sequential likelihood.
for record in records.values():
    if record["loss_function"] == "jaxcmr.loss.transform_sequence_likelihood.ExcludeTerminationLikelihoodLoss":
        record["loss_function"] = "jaxcmr.loss.sequence_likelihood.ExcludeTerminationLikelihoodLoss"
display_labels = {name: model_labels.get(name, name) for name in records}




7 — Establish matching observations, objectives and stopping rules
first = next(iter(records.values()))
selected_rows = sorted(first["selected_trial_indices"])
if (
    len(records) < 2
    or not selected_rows
    or len(set(selected_rows)) != len(selected_rows)
):
    raise ValueError(
        "Compare at least two pooled fits with a nonempty observation selection."
    )
for name, record in records.items():
    if record["fits"]["subject"] != [-1] or len(record["fitness"]) != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} is not a single pooled fit.")
    if (
        record.get("data_path", data_source) != data_source
        or sorted(record["selected_trial_indices"]) != selected_rows
    ):
        raise ValueError(f"{name}: observations or selected rows differ.")
    if (
        record["loss_function"] != first["loss_function"]
        or recorded_policy_path(record["components"])
        != recorded_policy_path(first["components"])
    ):
        raise ValueError("These fits do not use a common objective and stopping rule.")
comparison_mask = (
    jnp.zeros(len(subjects), dtype=bool).at[jnp.asarray(selected_rows)].set(True)
)
print(len(selected_rows), "shared lists; objective:", first["loss_function"])
print("Stopping policy:", recorded_policy_path(first["components"]))

title: Comparing pooled model fits
text:
Recalculate likelihoods
The notebook rebuilds each saved model and evaluates the recorded physical parameter values on the shared observations. This checks numerical consistency with the saved result. It does not rerun optimization or establish convergence to a global optimum. The displayed table is the historical output saved with this notebook. Running the cell recalculates the scores with the installed library.


9 — Check saved likelihoods against the current inputs
recalculated = {}
for name, record in records.items():
    model_factory = construct_model(record)
    features = load_features(record)
    loss_class = import_from_string(record["loss_function"])
    fixed = (
        record.get("fit_configuration", {})
        .get("parameters", {})
        .get("fixed", record["fixed"])
    )
    names = tuple(record["free"])
    evaluate = make_scipy_loss_fn(
        loss_class(model_factory, data, features),
        jnp.asarray(selected_rows),
        fixed,
        names,
    )
    values = jnp.asarray([record["fits"][key][0] for key in names])
    recalculated[name] = float(evaluate(values))
    if not np.isclose(recalculated[name], record["fitness"][0], rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-5):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{name}: saved NLL {record['fitness'][0]:.6f}, "
            f"recalculated NLL {recalculated[name]:.6f}."
        )
print(
    tabulate(
        [
            {
                "Model": display_labels[name],
                "Saved NLL": record["fitness"][0],
                "Recalculated NLL": recalculated[name],
            }
            for name, record in records.items()
        ],
        headers="keys",
        floatfmt=".6f",
    )
)

title: Comparing pooled model fits
section: Compare fit scores and search histories
text:
Compare fit scores and search histories
The table reports negative log likelihood, the number of free parameters, AIC and differences from the smallest AIC. AIC adds a parameter-count penalty to the likelihood score; lower values are preferred within this eligible comparison.
Inspect optimization histories alongside the score table: a poorer result may reflect an unsuccessful search. These are pooled fits, so model-score differences are not participant-level paired observations.


10 — Calculate and save pooled AIC comparisons
from jaxcmr.summarize import aic_scores

# Each pooled fit incurs one penalty, using its unscaled negative log likelihood.
comparison = [
    {
        "Model": display_labels[name],
        "Free parameters": len(record["free"]),
        "Negative log likelihood": recalculated[name],
        "AIC": float(aic_scores(recalculated[name], len(record["free"]))),
    }
    for name, record in records.items()
]
best = min(row["AIC"] for row in comparison)
for row in comparison:
    row["Delta AIC"] = row["AIC"] - best
print(tabulate(comparison, headers="keys", floatfmt=".3f"))
with (output_dir / "pooled_model_comparison.csv").open("w", newline="") as stream:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=list(comparison[0]))
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(comparison)

Compare saved predictions
The saved simulation settings are checked against the fitted models and simulation settings before plotting. Behavioral comparisons complement likelihood-based scores by showing where a model succeeds or fails.
The supplied responses were generated with observed recall lengths imposed. Their agreement in length is not a prediction of stopping. Repeated simulations retain the original participant IDs when computing summaries.


12 — Load the responses produced by the fitting or simulation procedure
simulations = {}
for name, record in records.items():
    path = resolve_project_path(simulation_paths[name], root_path)
    metadata = json.loads(path.with_suffix(".json").read_text())
    expected = {
        "data_path": data_source,
        "selected_trial_indices": selected_rows,
        "fits": record["fits"],
        "model_factory": record["model_factory"],
        "components": record["components"],
        "simulation_function": record["simulation_function"],
    }
    if any(metadata.get(key) != value for key, value in expected.items()):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{name}: saved responses belong to a different fit or observation selection."
        )
    simulated = load_data(str(path))
    if filter_repeated_recalls:
        simulated = simulated.copy()
        simulated["recalls"] = repetition.filter_repeated_recalls(simulated["recalls"])
    simulations[name] = simulated
    print(
        display_labels[name],
        "—",
        path,
        "— seed",
        metadata["seed"],
        "— repetitions",
        metadata["experiment_count"],
    )
figure_dir = resolve_project_path(figure_dir, root_path) if figure_dir is not None else output_dir
figure_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

comparison_groups = []
if redo_figures and simulations:
    observed = data.copy()
    if filter_repeated_recalls:

            {

On this page

    Inspect behavioral predictions

Use this procedure to estimate parameters for one or more specified models from your observations. It saves fit records that the simulation and model-comparison templates can read, and can also generate responses and behavioral figures.
A model specification describes the mechanism, fixed values and bounds for fitted parameters. Optimizer settings describe how the search is conducted. The defaults fit three related models to the supplied observations using one pooled parameter set per model. You can instead select one model, a subset of participants, or separate participant fits.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Fitting models
text:
Configure this run
Start with data_path, output_dir, the observation selection and model_configs. For each model, inspect the component choices, parameters["fixed"], parameters["free"] and their bounds. A one-entry model_configs dictionary runs one model and is also a useful independent batch job.
pooled=True estimates one parameter set across the selected participants; pooled=False estimates participant-specific sets. subject_indices refers to positions in the sorted participant-ID list, not to the IDs themselves. Splitting a pooled fit into participant jobs changes the scientific analysis.
Set search effort in fit_hyperparams, separately from model parameters. The default optimizer settings can take substantial time. redo_fits=False loads an existing file at the chosen fit path without checking compatibility; a missing file still starts optimization. Reuse only a fit you know matches this run. Set both redo_sims and redo_figures to False for a fit-only run. Use a distinct output folder or run tag for a new specification.
Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.

title: Fitting models
text:
Prepare the environment and inputs
Run the following setup cells once, then continue in order. The short installation cell runs only in Colab; local and Slurm runs use the environment you selected during Setup.
project_root anchors relative paths. When it is unset, Colab uses the current directory; elsewhere the notebook uses the enclosing Git project if present, or the current directory. Check the printed location. copy_example_inputs copies requested bundled examples there, reuses matching files, and refuses to overwrite conflicting files. Custom input paths remain your responsibility.


2 — Prepare the Colab environment
import sys

if "google.colab" in sys.modules:
    %pip install --upgrade "jaxcmr @ git+https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git@main"




3 — Import packages
import json

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from tabulate import tabulate

import jaxcmr
from jaxcmr import repetition
from jaxcmr.examples import copy_example_inputs
from jaxcmr.models import model_factory_from_paths
from jaxcmr.fitting import (
    make_scipy_loss_fn,
    parameters_for_subjects,
)
from jaxcmr.dataset import generate_trial_mask
from jaxcmr.helpers import import_from_string
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data, save_dict_to_hdf5
from jaxcmr.helpers import resolve_project_path, resolve_project_root
from jaxcmr.plotting import save_figure
from jaxcmr.plotting import iter_analysis_figures
from jaxcmr.simulation import (
    load_matching_simulation,
    simulate_dataset,
)


Feature composition stays explicit here. feature_column selects the categorical feature, and concat_features=True combines categorical columns before semantic columns. When concatenation is requested, supply both feature arrays; otherwise the configured concatenation fails rather than substituting a different feature set.


4 — Define feature loading and model construction
def load_features(spec):
    if spec.get("concat_features", False):
        semantic = np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["embedding_path"], root_path))
        categorical = np.load(
            resolve_project_path(spec["emotion_feature_path"], root_path)
        )[:, int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) : int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) + 1]
        return np.concatenate([categorical, semantic], axis=1)
    semantic = np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["embedding_path"], root_path)) if spec.get("embedding_path") else None
    categorical = (
        np.load(resolve_project_path(spec["emotion_feature_path"], root_path))[
            :,
            int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) : int(spec.get("feature_column", 6)) + 1,
        ]
        if spec.get("emotion_feature_path")
        else None
    )
    return categorical if categorical is not None else semantic


def construct_model(spec):
    return model_factory_from_paths(spec["model_factory"], spec["components"])




5 — Load observations and establish runtime settings
root_path = resolve_project_root(project_root)
print("Project directory:", root_path)

copy_example_inputs([data_path], base_dir=root_path)

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", enable_x64)
data_path = resolve_project_path(data_path, root_path)
output_dir = resolve_project_path(output_dir, root_path)
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
data = load_data(str(data_path))
data_source = (
    data_path.relative_to(root_path).as_posix()
    if data_path.is_relative_to(root_path)
    else str(data_path)
)
subjects = np.asarray(data["subject"]).ravel()

title: Fitting models
text:
Inspect the work unit
The next cells select observations, create output locations and report the participants, models and free-parameter counts. trial_query controls the fitting observations. analysis_trial_query later controls behavioral displays; it does not change the observations used to fit the model.
Check the printed selection before launching optimization. target_directory, fit_dir, simulation_dir and figure_dir override their respective default locations; changing output_dir alone does not redirect an explicit override.


8 — Select the participant work unit and observation trials
data_tag = data_tag or data_path.stem
subject_ids = np.unique(subjects)
if max_subjects:
    subject_ids = subject_ids[:max_subjects]
cohort_mask = generate_trial_mask(data, trial_query) & jnp.isin(
    data["subject"].ravel(), subject_ids
)
if subject_indices:
    subject_ids = subject_ids[np.asarray(subject_indices, dtype=int)]
comparison_mask = cohort_mask & jnp.isin(data["subject"].ravel(), subject_ids)
selected_rows = np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(comparison_mask)).tolist()
if not selected_rows:
    raise ValueError("The configured selection contains no observations.")
if not model_configs:
    raise ValueError("Supply at least one model configuration.")




9 — Prepare output directories
product_root = resolve_project_path(target_directory, root_path) if target_directory is not None else output_dir
fit_dir = resolve_project_path(fit_dir, root_path) if fit_dir is not None else product_root / "fits"
simulation_dir = (
    resolve_project_path(simulation_dir, root_path) if simulation_dir is not None else product_root / "simulations"
)
figure_dir = (
    resolve_project_path(figure_dir, root_path) if figure_dir is not None else product_root / "figures/fitting"
)
for directory in [fit_dir, simulation_dir, figure_dir]:
    directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)




10 — Summarize the selected work unit and model settings
print(
    f"Selected {len(selected_rows)} lists from {len(np.unique(subjects[selected_rows]))} participants."
)
display_labels = {name: spec.get("label", name) for name, spec in model_configs.items()}
print(
    tabulate(
        [
            {
                "Model": display_labels[name],
                "Free parameters": len(spec["parameters"]["free"]),
                "Seed": spec["seed"],
            }
            for name, spec in model_configs.items()
        ],
        headers="keys",
    )
)
