title: Templates
section: From a template to a run
text:
From a template to a run
Save downloaded notebooks in your working folder, beside data/. Open the folder in your notebook editor, select its Python environment, edit the parameters cell and run the notebook from top to bottom. Relative paths follow the project-directory rules below. Give independent runs distinct output folders or run names so their results do not overwrite one another.

Paths and working directories
The project_root parameter selects the base for all relative input and output paths:







Setting or execution context
Base directory




An explicit project_root
That directory; a relative value uses the kernel’s starting directory.


Local checkout, project_root=None
The enclosing Git root, found by the existing find_project_root() helper.


Standalone folder, project_root=None
The kernel’s working directory.


Colab, project_root=None
The runtime’s working directory.



The notebook reports the chosen directory. Running from templates/ or a nested prepared-job directory inside a checkout uses the same project inputs and outputs. When the kernel starts outside the project, supply project_root explicitly. The root belongs to your research project; it is not the installed JAXCMR package directory.
Absolute paths remain absolute, and ~ expands to your home directory. On Windows, "C:/Users/Alex/my-study" or r"C:\Users\Alex\my-study" works; avoid a partially specified drive path such as "C:my-study". UNC paths are supported on Windows. Relative defaults such as "data/Dupertuys2026.h5" work on both platforms. An absolute path from another computer must be updated there.
The input helper copies recognized relative example names into this same base on every platform. Custom files remain your responsibility; selecting an absolute custom path does not download an example over it. Path resolution happens after parameter injection and does not change the process’s working directory.


Saved products and regeneration
Copy the fit_paths printed by fitting into simulation, then supply the printed simulation_paths to model comparison or their values as analysis data_paths. The defaults continue to use the supplied examples until you replace them. For example, a one-model simulation job can use:
fit_paths = {"CMR": "results/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo_best_of_3.json"}
output_dir supplies default locations, but explicit directory settings take precedence:







Procedure
Directory precedence




Fitting
target_directory or output_dir supplies the product root; explicit fit_dir, simulation_dir and figure_dir override their defaults.


Simulation
Explicit simulation_dir and figure_dir override output_dir. The example sets simulation_dir="results/simulations".


Parameter shifting, model comparison and analyses
Explicit figure_dir overrides its default; summary tables use output_dir.



Give independent jobs distinct names or directories for every product they write. redo_fits=False loads an existing fit at the chosen path; you must establish that its model, parameters, participants, observations and input data match your intended run. Compatibility is not checked. A missing fit is still computed. After relevant changes, set redo_fits=True or choose a new output location. redo_sims=False permits matching response reuse; when predictions are requested, missing or stale responses are regenerated. Fitting is fit-only when both redo_sims and redo_figures are false. figure_str="" disables figure saving, but does not disable summary CSVs.
Reuse checks compare saved settings and, for fits, independently recalculate the objective. They do not detect edits to data or code in place. After such changes, set redo_fits=True and/or redo_sims=True for the affected calculations, or use a new output location. A matching path is not proof of matching file contents.
Settings are ordinary values: paths, numbers, lists, dictionaries and import names. Imports, trial masks and model construction happen afterward, using the effective values. The fitting template can select a model and its components, objective, fitted parameters, participant subset and displayed analyses. Analysis templates expose their trial selections and measure-specific settings. Their inputs are saved response files; preparing or running an analysis does not generate missing simulations.
Ordinary imports occupy their own cell after the optional Colab bootstrap. Derived paths, loading and calculations follow the injected parameters. figure_str="" displays figures without saving them; a nonempty name saves under figure_dir. The defaults provide explicit names for the worked examples. Subject-level CSV summaries use output_dir.
The analysis controls include repeated-item capacity (size), stopping mode, condition queries, category fields and labels, and plot limits. Category recall also accepts configured paired contrasts and contrasts of contrasts. Select these for the question being asked; the defaults leave the optional tests empty.
You can also supply settings externally. Quarto and Papermill use the same tagged cell. An override replaces a whole top-level value: to change one model, supply the complete model_configs dictionary for that work unit. Use fit_alg_path and fit_hyperparams to select and configure the optimizer. Analysis templates accept a list of response files (data_paths) and a matching list of names (data_labels). Each trial query applies to every file.


Execute a report with Quarto
With Quarto installed, you can execute a notebook with overrides and render its results to HTML. Python parameter injection uses Papermill, which the repository’s default uv sync already installs. For this example, run from the repository root and select the environment for Quarto using the command for your shell:

macOS / LinuxWindows PowerShell


export QUARTO_PYTHON="$(uv run python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')"


$env:QUARTO_PYTHON = (uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)")



Then run the same command on either platform:
quarto render templates/pnr.ipynb --execute -P query_recall_position:2 -P output_dir:results/pnr-third --output pnr-third.html
Quarto normally executes from the notebook’s directory; the template’s root lookup handles that. An injected project_root also works for notebooks prepared outside the project. The website build does not execute notebooks.
Output positions are zero-based, so 2 means the third response. Use --execute-params settings.yml for dictionaries or longer selections. The explicit --execute runs the notebook; rendering an .ipynb without it normally displays its stored results. The website displays saved example outputs.


Prepare independent jobs with Papermill
For a cluster batch, it can be useful to inspect the complete set of jobs before executing any of them. Papermill’s prepare_only=True creates a configured notebook for each job. From the repository root, the following Python cell prepares two fitting runs that differ only in optimization seed and output folder:


Prepare two fitting jobs without running them
from pathlib import Path
from copy import deepcopy
import nbformat
import papermill as pm

source = nbformat.read("templates/fitting.ipynb", as_version=4)
defaults = {}
parameter_cell = next(cell for cell in source.cells
                      if "parameters" in cell.metadata.get("tags", []))
# Evaluate only the parameter assignments, not the fitting procedure.
exec(parameter_cell.source, defaults)

jobs = Path("analyses/rendered")
jobs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for seed in [0, 1]:
    configs = deepcopy(defaults["model_configs"])
    for config in configs.values():
        config["seed"] = seed
    path = jobs / f"fitting_seed_{seed}.ipynb"
    prepared = pm.execute_notebook(
        "templates/fitting.ipynb", str(path),
        parameters={"model_configs": configs, "output_dir": f"results/fitting-seed-{seed}"},
        prepare_only=True,
    )
    # Stored example results are not results from this new job.
    for cell in prepared.cells:
        if cell.cell_type == "code":
            cell.outputs = []
            cell.execution_count = None
    nbformat.write(prepared, path)


To prepare one model per job, pass a one-entry model_configs dictionary. Preserve the project’s chosen job boundaries: a model collection does not require running every model in each scheduled job. Inspect the injected settings in each notebook. Execute one from the working folder with:
uv run papermill analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb --cwd .
The same prepared notebooks can be transferred with their inputs and run as separate Slurm jobs, using the project folder as the working directory. This keeps the prepared paths portable: set --cwd to the destination project folder, or inject its project_root when executing. Do not inject a local machine’s absolute root into jobs intended for a different machine. This matches the remote-cluster workflow: maintain a procedure, prepare concrete work units, then schedule their execution. Preparing jobs does not fit a model; rendering HTML is a separate presentation step.
For participant jobs, the fitting template uses pooled=False and subject_indices=[i], where i indexes the sorted participant IDs. Simulation and parameter exploration can instead vary seeds or parameter values. Choose the work unit around the scientific question and keep its inputs and outputs explicit. A fit-only job sets both redo_sims and redo_figures to False; later simulation can use its saved result.

title: Templates
text:
Modeling procedures
The example collection estimates nine continuous CMR parameters and ten for each eCMR variant, using the same observations and termination-excluded likelihood. The two eCMR specifications differ in whether emotional modulation also affects temporal association learning. The default simulator conditions on observed recall counts. Recall length, stopping distributions and pure-list category totals therefore are imposed; mixed-list category allocation and recall organization can vary.
Simulation and parameter shifting start from the supplied fits without optimization. The latter includes encoding-drift sweeps and a separate controlled temporal-emotional-modulation switch. Model comparison consumes the saved fits and responses. Its results describe pooled solutions, not independent participant estimates. Each procedure remains configurable for other inputs, models and scientific questions.

text:
Adapting a procedure
Each published notebook explains its required inputs, common settings, selection checks, calculation and saved outputs. Start with its settings cell, then run in order. You can read the explanatory text with code folded on the website or beside the executable cells in Jupyter and Colab.
Adapt the settings cell: input paths, trial selection, parameters and output folder. Check the meanings of item codes, participant identifiers, categories and response padding before interpreting results. Retain the same selection for comparisons that are intended to address the same observations.
Most analysis templates use data_path to compare conditions within one file and data_paths to compare files within each condition. The SPC template selects which curves share a figure with comparison. In SPC, use one-entry lists for a single file or condition. With comparison="conditions", the dataset label titles the figure and the condition labels identify its curves. Category-specific templates describe their additional panels alongside the calculations.
The remaining repository templates are research examples with varying dependencies and maintenance status. They remain at their original paths and are outside this prepared set.

Comparing observed and simulated SPCs
In the bundled Dupertuys example, the list_type field codes mixed lists as 1, pure emotional lists as 2, and pure neutral lists as 3. The SPC notebook starts with observed recall for each of those conditions. To overlay model predictions, supply the simulated response files alongside the observations. These settings include all three bundled models. For one model, keep its entry and the observed entry in both lists.
data_paths = [

]

Use this procedure to ask how category differences in recall vary across study positions. It reads response files with per-position category codes and saves category-specific serial position curves.
Each category has its own presentation opportunities at each position. An absent category-position combination is undefined, rather than evidence that recall probability is zero.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Serial position curves by category
text:

Use lag-conditional response probability (lag-CRP) to ask whether successive recalls favor nearby study positions, and whether forward and backward transitions differ. The procedure reads response files, compares chosen transitions with available opportunities, and saves a curve.
Positive lag means moving forward in the study list; negative lag means moving backward. Opportunity correction matters because positions near a list boundary do not offer the same possible lags.

title: Lag-conditional response probability
text:
Follow one transition
The table takes the first two recalls from an eligible list. It shows the next item chosen, each available study position, and its lag from the preceding recall. This makes the denominator visible: every available alternative contributes an opportunity, while the chosen transition contributes an actual event.
Later transitions have fewer alternatives because previously recalled items are removed. The full calculation applies the library’s repeated-item conventions; the small illustration selects an unrepeated study list.


8 — Count the choices available for one transition
selected = np.logical_or.reduce([np.asarray(mask) for mask in trial_masks])
eligible = selected & ((np.asarray(data["recalls"]) > 0).sum(axis=1) >= 2)
unrepeated = np.array(
    [
        len(np.unique(items[items > 0])) == np.count_nonzero(items)
        for items in presentations
    ]
)
eligible_rows = np.flatnonzero(eligible & unrepeated)
if not len(eligible_rows):
    print(
        "No unrepeated list with two recalls to illustrate; transition-based summaries are undefined for this selection."
    )
else:
    row = int(eligible_rows[0])
    recall = np.asarray(data["recalls"])[row].astype(int)
    recall = recall[recall > 0]
    previous, chosen = recall[:2]
    available = np.flatnonzero(presentations[row] > 0) + 1
    available = available[available != previous]
    print(
        tabulate(
            {
                "Available study position": available,
                "Lag from previous recall": available - previous,
                "Chosen next": available == chosen,
            },
            headers="keys",
            floatfmt=".4g",
        )
    )
    print(f"Observed transition: {previous} to {chosen}; lag = {chosen - previous:+d}")

For each participant, counts of actual transitions are divided by available opportunities at each lag. The figure summarizes these participant curves with bootstrap intervals. An unavailable lag is undefined, not a zero-probability observation.

Inspect one distance rank
The illustration compares a chosen next item’s distance with the alternatives still available. Closer choices receive larger ranks, with midpoint ties. A score of 1 is the closest rank and 0 the farthest; with fewer than two alternatives the score is undefined.
Under uniform choice among available alternatives, the reference is 0.5. This reference concerns ordering according to your matrix, not an independently established measure of semantic organization.

title: Temporal organization scores
text:
Illustrate an item-midrank transition
The table shows alternatives for the first transition in an eligible unrepeated list. The displayed score uses item midranks: each available item remains a separate alternative, and equally distant items receive midpoint ties. Higher scores favor nearer items; a transition with no alternative choice has no rank.
This illustration always uses item midranks. The aggregate default below is rank_method="lag_bins", the historical implementation that ranks available lag bins. Its handling of alternatives and ties differs. Set "item_midrank" only when that definition is intended and your study identities are unique.


8 — Rank one transition among its alternatives
selected = np.logical_or.reduce([np.asarray(mask) for mask in trial_masks])
eligible = selected & ((np.asarray(data["recalls"]) > 0).sum(axis=1) >= 2)
unrepeated = np.array(
    [
        len(np.unique(items[items > 0])) == np.count_nonzero(items)
        for items in presentations
    ]
)
eligible_rows = np.flatnonzero(eligible & unrepeated)
if not len(eligible_rows):
    print(
        "No unrepeated list with two recalls to illustrate; transition-based summaries are undefined for this selection."
    )
else:
    row = int(eligible_rows[0])
    recall = np.asarray(data["recalls"])[row].astype(int)
    recall = recall[recall > 0]
    previous, chosen = recall[:2]
    available = np.flatnonzero(presentations[row] > 0) + 1
    available = available[available != previous]
    print(
        tabulate(
            {
                "Available study position": available,
                "Lag from previous recall": available - previous,
                "Chosen next": available == chosen,
            },
            headers="keys",
            floatfmt=".4g",

    )
    print(f"Observed transition: {previous} to {chosen}; lag = {chosen - previous:+d}")

    distances = np.abs(available - previous)
    score = percentile_rank(jnp.asarray(abs(chosen - previous)), jnp.asarray(distances))
    print(f"Rank score for this transition: {float(score):.3f}")

Use this procedure to investigate what a fitted model does when selected parameters change. It loads saved baselines, simulates both the baseline and controlled changes on the same selected lists, and saves responses and comparisons.
This is a mechanism check: other parameters retain their fitted values. A parameter change may alter behavior while making the model fit the observations less well. To ask how well a different specification can fit after all free parameters adapt, use the fitting procedure instead.

title: Exploring parameter effects
text:
Configure this run
Replace fit_paths with the baselines you want to investigate. A sweep names a baseline through fit, one parameter, and its values; each value is applied to a fresh copy of that baseline. Separate sweeps do not form a Cartesian product.
Use parameter_interventions for a named set of simultaneous overrides to one baseline. For example, two mechanism switches can be changed together while every other parameter stays fixed. Choose values appropriate to the model, and keep a separate output folder for each investigation. experiment_count and simulation_seed control repeated simulation, not fitting.
Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.

def check_participant_fit(
    participant_record,
    reference_record,
    specification_keys,
    model_name,
):
    """Reject incompatible model specifications and pooled records."""
    if any(
        participant_record.get(key) != reference_record.get(key)
        for key in specification_keys
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{model_name}: participant fits have incompatible model or input specifications."
        )
    participant_ids = participant_record["fits"]["subject"]
    if participant_record.get("pooled", False) or -1 in participant_ids:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{model_name}: directories must contain participant fits, not pooled fits."
        )




7 — Define participant-file combination
def combine_participant_fits(participant_records, data, model_name):
    """Combine compatible participant estimates without losing their identities."""
    subjects = np.asarray(data["subject"]).ravel()
    specification_keys = (
        "model_factory",
        "components",
        "simulation_function",
        "loss_function",
        "data_path",
        "fixed",
        "free",
        "embedding_path",
        "emotion_feature_path",
        "feature_column",
        "concat_features",
    )
    reference_record = participant_records[0]
    combined_parameters = combine_participant_parameters(
        [record["fits"] for record in participant_records]
    )
    selected_rows = set()
    for participant_record in participant_records:
        check_participant_fit(
            participant_record,
            reference_record,
            specification_keys,
            model_name,
        )
        participant_ids = participant_record["fits"]["subject"]
        if "selected_trial_indices" in participant_record:
            rows = participant_record["selected_trial_indices"]
            if not np.isin(subjects[rows], participant_ids).all():
                raise ValueError(
                    f"{model_name}: recorded observation rows belong to another participant."
                )
        else:
            mask = generate_trial_mask(
                data,
                participant_record.get(
                    "trial_query", participant_record.get("data_query")
                ),
            )
            rows = np.flatnonzero(
                np.asarray(mask) & np.isin(subjects, participant_ids)
            ).tolist()
        selected_rows.update(rows)
    combined_record = {
        key: reference_record[key]
        for key in specification_keys
        if key in reference_record
    }
    combined_record.update(
        name=model_name,
        label=reference_record.get("label", model_name),
        pooled=False,
        fits=combined_parameters,
        selected_trial_indices=sorted(selected_rows),
    )
    # Preserve boolean settings as recorded before the fitter's numeric conversion.
    combined_record["fixed"] = (
        reference_record.get("fit_configuration", {})
        .get("parameters", {})
        .get("fixed", reference_record["fixed"])
    )
    return combined_record

title: Simulating from saved fits
text:
Generate and save responses
Each repetition uses the selected experimental lists and keeps the original participant identity. simulation_seed controls random sampling; changing it asks for another realization of the same configured model.
The supplied fits use a simulator that forces observed recall lengths. Agreement in total recall or stopping is consequently imposed. To use a different simulator, set sim_alg_path and check that it answers your intended question. Saved responses have a JSON file of simulation settings; both files are used when checking whether a previous simulation can be reused.
With redo_sims=False, matching settings allow saved responses to be reused. Changes to data or model code in place are not detected: set redo_sims=True after those changes.


12 — Prepare participant parameters and simulation settings
simulation_inputs = {}
for model_name, fit_record in records.items():
    model_factory = construct_model(fit_record)
    features = load_features(fit_record)
    selected_trials = selections[model_name]
    is_pooled = fit_record.get("pooled", fit_record["fits"]["subject"] == [-1])
    participant_ids = jnp.unique(data["subject"].ravel()[selected_trials])
    subject_parameters = parameters_for_subjects(fit_record, participant_ids)
    configuration = {
        "fits": fit_record["fits"],
        "pooled": is_pooled,
        "jax_enable_x64": enable_x64,
        "jaxcmr_version": jaxcmr.__version__,
        "model_factory": fit_record["model_factory"],
        "components": fit_record["components"],
        "simulation_function": fit_record["simulation_function"],
        "data_path": data_source,
        "selected_trial_indices": np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(selected_trials)).tolist(),
        "embedding_path": fit_record.get("embedding_path", ""),
        "emotion_feature_path": fit_record.get("emotion_feature_path", ""),
        "feature_column": fit_record.get("feature_column", 6),
        "concat_features": fit_record.get("concat_features", False),
        "seed": simulation_seed,
        "experiment_count": experiment_count,
    }

    for key in ("embedding_path", "emotion_feature_path"):
        if configuration[key]:
            feature_path = resolve_project_path(configuration[key], root_path)
            configuration[key] = (feature_path.relative_to(root_path).as_posix()
                          if feature_path.is_relative_to(root_path) else str(feature_path))
    simulation_inputs[model_name] = {
        "model_factory": model_factory,
        "features": features,
        "parameters": subject_parameters,
        "trial_mask": selected_trials,
        "configuration": configuration,
    }




13 — Generate or reuse matching responses and save them
simulations = {}
for model_name, prepared in simulation_inputs.items():
    model_factory = prepared["model_factory"]
    features = prepared["features"]
    subject_parameters = prepared["parameters"]
    selected_trials = prepared["trial_mask"]
    configuration = prepared["configuration"]
    simulation_path = simulation_paths[model_name]
    simulated = None
    if not redo_sims:
        simulated = load_matching_simulation(simulation_path, configuration)
    if simulated is None:
        simulated = simulate_dataset(
            model_factory,
            data,
            features,
            subject_parameters,
            selected_trials,
            experiment_count=experiment_count,
            rng=jax.random.PRNGKey(simulation_seed),
            simulate_trial_fn=import_from_string(configuration["simulation_function"]),
        )
        simulation_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        save_dict_to_hdf5(simulated, str(simulation_path))
        simulation_path.with_suffix(".json").write_text(
            json.dumps(
                {
                    **configuration,
                    "jaxcmr_version": jaxcmr.__version__,
                    "jax_version": jax.__version__,
                },
                indent=2,
            )
            + "\n"
        )
        print("Saved responses:", simulation_path)
    else:
        print("Loaded matching responses:", simulation_path)
    if filter_repeated_recalls:
        simulated = simulated.copy()
        simulated["recalls"] = repetition.filter_repeated_recalls(simulated["recalls"])
    simulations[model_name] = simulated
print(
    "simulation_paths =",
    {model_name: str(path) for model_name, path in simulation_paths.items()},
)

Use this procedure to describe where recorded recall sequences end, either as a distribution of sequence lengths or as the probability of stopping after reaching each position. It reads observed or simulated responses and saves a figure for the selected modes and conditions.
Recording capacity limits what can be inferred from the final bin. Also check how simulated responses were produced: the supplied simulations impose observed recall lengths, so their agreement here does not demonstrate a model’s ability to predict stopping.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

Choose response files and conditions. mode="simple" shows the proportion of sequences ending at each length; mode="conditional" divides endings by sequences that reached that position. Supply both in a list to inspect both views.

Keep all editable settings in this tagged cell. Later cells derive paths and selections after any Papermill overrides.


1 — Set the parameters for this run
# Inputs and saved results — change these for your project.

text:
Prepare the environment and inputs
Run the following setup cells once, then continue in order. The short installation cell runs only in Colab; local and Slurm runs use the environment you selected during Setup.
project_root anchors relative paths. When it is unset, Colab uses the current directory; elsewhere the notebook uses the enclosing Git project if present, or the current directory. Check the printed location. copy_example_inputs copies requested bundled examples there, reuses matching files, and refuses to overwrite conflicting files. Custom input paths remain your responsibility.


2 — Prepare the Colab environment
import sys

if "google.colab" in sys.modules:
    %pip install --upgrade "jaxcmr @ git+https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git@main"




3 — Import packages
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from jaxcmr.analyses.termination_probability import plot_termination_probability
from jaxcmr.dataset import select_conditions
from jaxcmr.examples import copy_example_inputs
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data
from jaxcmr.helpers import resolve_project_path, resolve_project_root
from jaxcmr.plotting import save_figure
from jaxcmr.plotting import comparison_panels

title: When recall ends
text:
Select the observations
select_conditions returns the masks and participant coverage without altering your data. Check the printed list and participant counts before interpreting the results. Queries are Python expressions evaluated with the dataset named data; replace the supplied condition codes with those in your data. trial_query overrides the list of trial_queries and uses selection_label.
With data_path set, the notebook reads that file and compares conditions. With data_path=None, data_paths and data_labels produce one panel per condition comparing datasets—even if the list contains just one file. Labels must correspond to the supplied selections and files.


4 — Resolve input paths, conditions and output settings
root_path = resolve_project_root(project_root)
print("Project directory:", root_path)

copy_example_inputs([data_path] if data_path is not None else data_paths, base_dir=root_path)

output_dir = resolve_project_path(output_dir, root_path)

    resolve_project_path(figure_dir, root_path)
    if figure_dir is not None
    else output_dir
)

queries = trial_queries if trial_query is None else [trial_query]
condition_labels = labels if trial_query is None else [selection_label]
input_paths = [data_path] if data_path is not None else data_paths
input_paths = [resolve_project_path(path, root_path) for path in input_paths]
input_labels = [selection_label] if data_path is not None else data_labels
if len(queries) != len(condition_labels) or len(input_paths) != len(input_labels):
    raise ValueError("Supply a label for each input and each condition query.")




5 — Load the supplied response datasets
datasets = [load_data(str(path), max_subjects=max_subjects) for path in input_paths]




6 — Select observations and report participant counts
selected_conditions = [
    select_conditions(dataset, queries, complete_lists_only=complete_lists_only)
    for dataset in datasets
]
masks_by_dataset = [[condition.mask for condition in group] for group in selected_conditions]
for dataset_label, group in zip(input_labels, selected_conditions):

        print(

title: When recall ends
text:
Interpret the stopping summaries
For a stored recall array of width K, the plotted lengths run from 0 to a final K−1+ bin. That final bin combines sequences ending there with sequences filling the recording capacity. The shaded region marks this limit; it cannot distinguish a voluntary stop from a recording cutoff.
The simple mode uses all selected sequences as its denominator. The conditional mode uses sequences that reached the relevant position. A position that was never reached has an undefined conditional probability. Participant summaries and bootstrap intervals are then plotted.


7 — Prepare the condition and dataset comparison panels
panels = comparison_panels(
    datasets, masks_by_dataset, input_labels, condition_labels,
    mode="conditions" if data_path is not None else "datasets",
    selection_label=selection_label,
)

modes = [mode] if isinstance(mode, str) else mode
mode_panels = []
for panel in panels:
    for display_mode in modes:
        mode_panels.append({**panel, "mode": display_mode})
panels = mode_panels




8 — Calculate, plot and save the selected comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(panels), 1, figsize=(8, 3.8 * len(panels)), squeeze=False)
for ax, panel in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
    panel_data = panel["datasets"]
    panel_masks = panel["trial_masks"]
    curve_labels = panel["labels"]
    title = panel["title"]
    display_mode = panel["mode"]
    plot_termination_probability(
        panel_data,
        panel_masks,
        mode=display_mode,
        labels=curve_labels,
        contrast_name=contrast_name,
        color_cycle=color_cycle,
        confidence_level=confidence_level,
        axis=ax,
        bootstrap_seed=plot_seed,
    )
    title += f" — {display_mode}"
    widths = {dataset["recalls"].shape[1] for dataset in panel_data}
    if len(widths) != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            "Use matching recording capacities for overlaid terminal bins."
        )
    capacity = widths.pop()
    ax.set_xticks(
        np.arange(1, capacity + 1),
        [str(i) for i in range(capacity - 1)] + [f"{capacity - 1}+"],
    )
    ax.set_xlabel(f"Recorded recalls ({capacity - 1}+ = terminal recording bin)")
    ax.axvspan(capacity - 0.5, capacity + 0.5, color="grey", alpha=0.18)
    ax.set_title(title)

    if ax.get_legend_handles_labels()[1]:
        ax.legend(title=contrast_name)
    if ylim is not None:
        ax.set_ylim(ylim[0], ylim[1])
    if yticks is not None:
        ax.set_yticks(yticks)
if figure_str:
    save_figure(str(figure_dir), figure_str, figure=plt.gcf())
else:
    plt.gcf().tight_layout()
plt.show()

Run memory-search models through study and recall.
A model defines how experiences change memory and how memory determines the probabilities of subsequent responses. This module uses those operations to present study lists and generate recall sequences. A dataset supplies the study lists, participant identities and trial metadata; observed recalls can also supply a first response or determine which generated response slots are retained.
Use simulate_dataset to generate responses for selected trials, optionally repeating each trial. Use simulate_parameter_sweep to run those trials at several values of one parameter. Both use MemorySearchSimulator, which can also be prepared once and called directly with different parameter sets and random keys.
These dataset operations build on smaller operations that can be used directly:
During retrieval, response codes identify items within a list. Returned datasets express recalls as study positions. When an item appears more than once, its recall is recorded at the first matching study position. Study metadata is retained; fields describing the original responses are removed.
load_matching_simulation supports reuse of saved responses by checking their recorded settings against the requested settings. The caller decides when to reuse responses and handles saving, parameter fitting and behavioral analysis.

On this page
  
    
    
    Finding study occurrences
    Identifying and handling repeated recalls
    Constructing shuffled controls
    API entries
    
    item_to_study_positions
    equivalent_study_positions
    has_repeats_per_row
    recalls_to_first_study_positions
    filter_repeated_recalls
    make_control_dataset
Recall data use study positions to identify recalled items.
When an item appears more than once, several positions refer to the same item. For the study list [A, B, A], a recall recorded as position 3 refers to the item presented at positions 1 and 3.
This module finds those positions, converts recalls to each item’s first study position, and identifies repeated responses. Removing a repeated response replaces its code with zero; it does not shift later responses.
make_control_dataset constructs shuffled controls by pairing recall sequences from lists without repeated items (“pure” lists) with study layouts containing repeats (“mixed” lists). Pairings stay within participants, and each mixed trial appears once per shuffle. The recall codes are then interpreted using the paired mixed-list layout.

Data formats and callable interfaces for recall models, simulation and fitting.
RecallDataset describes the arrays recorded on each trial, and Parameters maps parameter names to scalar model values. Array annotations specify the dtype and dimensions a caller supplies.
Memory, Context, TerminationPolicy and ResponsePolicy describe components used to build a model. MemorySearch describes how a model experiences study items and produces recall responses. A MemorySearchModelFactory constructs that model for a particular trial. A TrialSimulator uses it to carry out a study and recall procedure.
For fitting, a LossFactory constructs an objective for a dataset. LossFn scores candidate parameter sets, and a FittingAlgorithm returns estimates and objective values in a FitResult. These protocols specify the operations an implementation must supply. A model, loss or fitter can satisfy its protocol without inheriting from it.

jaxcmr.typing.RecallDataset: TypedDict

Trial-indexed arrays for free or serial recall experiments.
The required fields are subject, listLength, pres_itemnos, and recalls. Their annotated shapes and integer dtypes appear below; zeros pad item and recall sequences.
pres_itemids identifies items across lists and is required by semantic models and analyses, but not by every recall dataset. Other named fields are optional. Read and save array files, resolve project paths, and support configured calls.
load_hdf5_arrays reads named arrays from JAXCMR’s HDF5 layout; load_data uses it to load recall datasets and optionally limit participants. save_dict_to_hdf5 writes arrays in the same layout. Use the generic reader for observations that do not have the fields of a recall dataset.

All three return pathlib.Path objects.
import_from_string resolves dotted Python names for configured calls, and format_floats formats numeric labels. Figure saving lives in jaxcmr.plotting; dataset operations live in jaxcmr.dataset.

    make_factory
    RecallAnalysisFn
    MemorySearchSpcMseLoss

Fit a model to behavioral measures calculated from observed and simulated recall.
Use MemorySearchSpcMseLoss when the target is recall probability by study position, or MemorySearchCatSpcMseLoss when the target is a separate curve for each category. To fit another measure, give MemorySearchMseLoss the analysis you use on observed recall. It applies that function to the observed dataset and to a simulated dataset with the same study lists.
Each candidate parameter set generates several recalls per trial. The model can stop early, and only response slots up to the observed response count are retained. Candidates use the same random keys. With several analyses, all predicted summaries come from the same simulated responses. make_factory lets you give a fitter that combination of analyses, their weights, and the scales used to compare their squared errors. Discrete recall sampling makes this loss suitable for derivative-free search.

text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Trial model
    Model factory
    API entries
    
    CMR
    make_factory
Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) represents each item once per trial. Studying an item moves temporal context toward that item’s associated context and strengthens the associations in both directions. A second presentation updates the same item’s associations.
At recall, the current context cues the available items. By default CMR chooses whether to stop, then selects an item in proportion to its support. Each policy returns the probabilities of STOP and the individual items. Simulation samples from them and likelihood reads the observed entry. Recalling an item reinstates its associated context, changing the cue for the next response.

Positional CMR learns an association at each study position. On a list [A, B, A], context can cue both the first and third positions. Their supports add to give the support for recalling A.

Ordinary CMR learns associations between items and temporal context. Its factory combines two associative memories, a context, and a response policy. The model interface describes the events that simulators and losses use.

Repeated presentations
Positional CMR learns an association at each study position. If an item occurs twice, both positions can contribute to the probability of recalling that item. The response policy evaluates the available study positions. Positional CMR sums their weights by item code before assigning item probabilities. In the blended model each route first gives its own probability to STOP and each item. When an item is recalled, those route probabilities also determine how much each route contributes to reinstatement.
The RepFR model configurations identify the reinforcement and reinstatement variants used in that project’s comparisons.

A trial records items in study order. A model looks up a recalled item by its within-list code. A word pool uses a third index, the item’s vocabulary ID.

    RawSupportRatioSoftmaxChoice

Use retrieval evidence to decide whether recall continues. Each studied item contributes its current support to one of two sums, according to whether it can still be recalled. More available support relative to unavailable support makes stopping less likely.
The two response policies use the same stopping probability. If recall continues, RawSupportRatioSoftmaxChoice applies a softmax to the available items’ evidence. RawSupportRatioRelativeChoice uses the model’s own candidate weights, including its choice sensitivity and any semantic weighting.

jaxcmr.components.support_ratio.SupportsStudiedEvidenceAndWeights: Protocol

Supply raw evidence for stopping and candidate weights for item choice.
Kragel et al. (2015, equations 8–10) sum item support before calculating STOP and use proportional choice among the remaining items. Zhang et al. (2023) use a support ratio for STOP and a softmax for item choice. The policies here use a configurable stopping baseline and a floor of 1e-6 on each studied item’s contribution to the ratio. Kragel et al. · Zhang et al.

On this page
  
    
    
    Context
    Associative memory
    Choosing the next response
    Stopping rules

title: Model components
text:
Context
Temporal context updates the current context from an input pattern and a drift rate. Models that introduce fresh out-of-list units also require a context initialized with room for those units. Context interface

title: Model components
text:
Associative memory
Linear memory adds associations to a matrix. Instance memory keeps a trace for each association. Suppose a cue matches two stored inputs with strengths 2 and 1. Linear retrieval weights their outputs by 2 and 1. Instance retrieval at sensitivity one weights them by 1 and 0.5. Its probe_without_scale method recovers the raw weights.
Both modules supply init_mfc for item-to-context memory and init_mcf for context-to-item memory. Memory interface

title: Model components
text:
Choosing the next response
Response policies assign probabilities to STOP and each item. Ordinary CMR can choose a stopping probability separately, compete STOP against items, or use an experimental diffusion race. Semantic and positional models can use their own candidate weights with scheduled stopping or recall until exhaustion. Models that supply item evidence on a common scale can use the raw support ratio to decide when to stop. Direct competition with STOP requires raw candidate evidence. A terminal-item model can also retrieve a learned STOP.

title: Model components
text:
Stopping rules
The stopping rules use candidate availability, output position, support for recalled items, or an explicit STOP candidate. Each entry identifies the information its rule needs from a model.

title: Model components
text:
Preparing trial inputs
The trial-input operations match local item codes to vocabulary IDs and valence categories. Semantic and emotional model factories use these rows to look up the recalled item even when it appeared more than once.

Lag-conditional response probabilities for selected recall events.
Suppose the recalls are A, B, C and only the transition into C is selected. B still leaves the set of available items and becomes the starting point for the transition to C. The event mask controls which transitions add to the actual and available lag counts. Removing B from the recall sequence would instead create a different transition, from A to C.
Use crp to pool those counts across trials. A source field can select transitions by the previous item’s condition. A target field gives each target condition its own lag opportunities. When supplying both, request one source value at a time. plot_crp calculates participant curves before averaging them.

    plot_conditional_corec_by_cat
Joint and conditional recall of pairs of different study items.
corec_by_lag measures the probability that both items in an eligible pair were recalled. conditional_corec_by_lag conditions on recalling the earlier study position’s item. conditional_corec_by_cat instead selects recalled anchors by category and compares same-category with different-category targets.
Responses identify items through study positions. A recalled item credits all of its presentations, but two occurrences of that same item never form an eligible pair. Padding is excluded. Dataset calculations pool pair counts; plotters calculate each participant’s probability before averaging participants. Zero-opportunity groups remain undefined.

    CueCenteredTabulation
Recall probability by study lag from an external retrieval cue.
Suppose A, B, C, D were studied in order. If the previous recall was A, the cue is D, and the response is C, the cue-centered lag is −1. The same response would have lag +2 measured from the previous recall. The cues in cue_clips are supplied separately for each output position.
cue_centered_crp divides observed cue-to-response lag counts by the opportunities for each lag among the items still available. Repeated cue or response items can correspond to several study positions. The event mask selects which responses contribute counts. Each valid response updates availability for later recalls, including responses to an unscored cue.

Proximity of each recalled item to the previous recall in a distance matrix.
For each transition, the previous item’s row of the matrix supplies a distance to every available study item. The chosen distance is ranked among those alternatives. The closest scores 1 and the farthest 0 when distances are distinct. Tied items share their mean rank. Uniform choice among the available items gives an expected score of 0.5.
Use distrank for one mean rank per trial and subject_distrank for the mean of the defined trial scores per participant. Transitions with fewer than two available items contribute no rank. The global item identifiers in pres_itemids are one-based, so item 1 corresponds to the first row and column of the matrix.

Output positions at which a chosen study item is recalled.
When does the first item on a list come back? With query_study_position=0, each point on the curve is an output position for that first item. On a trial with study list A, B, C and recalls C, A, the first item contributes at output position 2. If the item was studied more than once, a recall recorded at any of its study positions identifies the same item.
simple_nth_item_recall_curve uses all trials containing the queried study position as the denominator at every output. conditional_nth_item_recall_curve starts with those trials and, at each later output, counts only trials where the item had yet to be recalled and the preceding output was nonzero. The two plotters calculate their respective curves per participant before averaging.

Recall of a studied item in the wrong output position.
For the study list A, B, C, D and responses B, C, blank, blank, the first two output positions each receive an order error. The last two receive zero. trial_order_error_rate flags a response when its item belongs to the list but was studied elsewhere. A repeated item is correct in any of its assigned positions.
order_error_rate averages these flags over all trials at each position. Trials with a blank or an intrusion at that position contribute zero and remain in the denominator. plot_order_error_rate averages participant rates.

On this page

    relative_srac
    tabulate_trial
    plot_relative_srac
    Tabulation
Recall of study items immediately after their study predecessors.
For the study list A, B, C, D, suppose a participant recalls B, then C. Relative serial accuracy credits C at study position 3 because B immediately preceded C during both study and recall. Strict serial accuracy would require C in output position 3. The first study position earns relative credit when its item is the first recall.
tabulate_trial marks the study positions that meet this rule. When an item appears several times, each occurrence can supply a matching neighbor. relative_srac averages those indicators across trials, and plot_relative_srac averages the participant curves.
A zero-coded blank currently indexes the last study item during transition scoring. For the example above, adding trailing zeros after B, C also credits D. This can inflate accuracy at the final study position.

    RepCRPTabulation
Recall transitions out of an item studied more than once.
Consider the study list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H. If X is recalled and H comes next, H is seven positions after the first X and one after the second. The same response contributes to lag +7 on the first-presentation curve and lag +1 on the second.
tabulate_trial counts actual and available lags separately from each presentation of a qualifying repeated item. repcrp pools these counts across trials before dividing. Comparing the curves shows where subsequent recalls fall relative to each presentation. The observed response identifies the item X and leaves its retrieved occurrence unknown.

    NeighborCRPTabulation
Recall transitions between the neighborhoods of two presentations of an item.
In the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, C immediately follows the first X. When C is recalled, the analysis can measure the next recall relative to the second X. A transition from C to H then has lag +1 because H follows the second X.
repneighborcrp divides these observed lags by the lags available from the comparison presentation. Choose the direction to start with neighbors of the first presentation, start with neighbors of the second, or combine both. use_lag2 also admits a starting item two positions after a presentation. X itself need never be recalled.

Strict serial accuracy for successive presentations of a repeated item.
Suppose a participant studies A, X, B, X and recalls A, X before stopping. The first presentation of X was recalled in its assigned output slot. The second was missed. This trial contributes one correct response out of one opportunity for the first presentation, and zero out of one for the second.
trial_repsrac_counts groups the position scores from trial_srac by occurrence number for items studied more than once. repsrac pools correct responses and opportunities across trials before dividing. An occurrence number with no opportunities receives a score of zero.

    RepCRPTabulation
Lag of the first qualifying transition from a repeated item during serial recall.
For the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, suppose the participant starts A, B, X, H. The run up to X follows study order. The transition from X to H is scored even though H breaks that order. It contributes lag +7 from the first X and +1 from the second. Each trial supplies at most one such transition. The first recall initializes the run, and order checks begin with the second response. To require a correct first recall, select those trials before calculating the curve.
repcrp pools the actual and possible lags from each presentation across trials. In this serial measure the possible lags are based on the full study layout. The free-recall measure in analyses.repcrp removes recalled items from the available alternatives.

On this page

    fixed_pres_spc
    spc
    plot_spc
Recall probability by study position.
The serial position curve (SPC) shows how often participants recall the item studied at each position, wherever it appears in the response sequence. On a trial with study list A, B, C and recalls C, A, positions 1 and 3 each receive one count. If the same item appeared at several study positions, recalling it once credits each of those positions. Recalling it again adds no further credit.
spc divides the count at each position by the number of trials with an item at that position. plot_spc calculates this curve separately for each participant and plots their mean. For fixed-length lists of distinct items, fixed_pres_spc computes the curve directly from position-coded recalls.

text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Means and intervals
    Comparisons
    API entries
    
    mean_interval
    compare_paired
    compare_to_reference
Summarize participant scores and compare paired measurements.
mean_interval reports a mean and bootstrap interval from independent observations, usually one score per participant. compare_to_reference and compare_paired report means, differences, t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in DataFrames. These operations use finite observations and give each included participant equal weight.
Calculate participant scores in the analysis module before using these operations. Paired arrays must have the same participants in the same order. Each comparison uses its own complete pairs, including for its marginal means. The tests are two-sided and their p-values are not adjusted for multiplicity. They answer different questions: the t-test concerns the mean difference; the signed-rank test concerns a distribution of differences symmetric about zero.
These NumPy/SciPy reporting operations run outside JAX compilation.

Serial accuracy and output-position measures retain their own response-order rules. Each entry describes the observations and denominator used by its calculation.

    CueCenteredLagRankTabulation
Rank the proximity of a recalled item to an external cue.
Suppose A, B, C, D were studied in order and a cue identifies D. A response of C lies one study position from that cue. To score it, the analysis ranks its absolute lag among the distinct absolute lags available from D at that moment. The closest lag scores 1 and the farthest scores 0 when at least two different lags are available.
cue_centered_lagrank returns one mean rank per trial and subject_cue_centered_lagrank averages the defined trial scores within participants. For the probability of moving in each direction and by each lag from the cue, use cue_centered_crp.
This experimental analysis has a provisional interface and interpretation.

text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Calculations
    Figures
    API entries
    
    log_odds_crp
    plot_log_odds_crp
Compare recall at each lag with recall at a chosen reference lag.
log_odds_crp first computes the ordinary lag-CRP across the supplied trials. At each lag it subtracts the log odds at the reference lag from the log odds at that lag. A positive contrast means greater odds than at the reference. The calculation bounds probabilities away from zero and one before converting to log odds. If the reference has no opportunities, the entire contrast curve is undefined.
plot_log_odds_crp computes the contrast separately for each participant before averaging. Call log_odds_crp directly to transform a pooled curve.
This experimental analysis has a provisional interface and interpretation.

title: jaxcmr.experimental.prepared_fitting
text:
On this page
  
    
    
    Prepared optimization
    API entries
    
    PreparedScipyLBFGSB
    PreparedScipyTrustConstr
Fit a differentiable loss to observations the caller has already selected.
For participant fits, select one participant’s trials and prepare a PreparedLoss that scores candidate parameters against those trials. Pass it to PreparedScipyLBFGSB.fit or PreparedScipyTrustConstr.fit with the participant ID. Each call returns one fit row for those observations.
A fitter can be used again with the next participant’s prepared loss. warmup compiles the evaluator before fitting when preparation and fit time need to be measured separately. Compatible observations and the same evaluation function can share that compilation. Parameter bounds, restarts and result rows follow the conventions of the dataset-based gradient fitters.

Temporal proximity of the next recall to each presentation of a repeated item.
In the list A, B, X, C, D, E, F, G, X, H, a transition from X to H covers seven positions from the first X and one from the second. Each distance is ranked among the distinct absolute lags still available from that presentation. A score near one places the response among the closest available lags. The two scores describe alternative reference positions for the same observed transition.
replagrank returns mean ranks by trial and presentation number. subject_rep_lagrank summarizes those trial scores for each participant. The corresponding repcrp curves retain the direction and size of individual lags.
This experimental analysis has a provisional interface and interpretation.

    TargetEnrichmentTabulation
Lag-CRP target enrichment.
Computes whether recalled targets at each lag are enriched for a target condition relative to the available targets at that same lag. This is a CRP-like diagnostic with a zero baseline: positive values mean the actual transitions at a lag select the target value more often than expected from lag-specific availability.
Experimental analysis; its interface and interpretation may change.

title: Serial position curves
text:
Choose the lists to compare
List each response file once and give it a label. Write one trial query per condition using fields shared by the files, and supply the condition names in the same order. To use all eligible lists as one condition, set trial_queries = [None] and labels = ["All lists"].


Select datasets, conditions and outputs
data_paths = ["data/Dupertuys2026.h5"]
data_labels = ["Observed"]
trial_queries = ["data['list_type'] == 1", "data['list_type'] == 2", "data['list_type'] == 3"]
labels = ["Mixed", "Pure emotional", "Pure neutral"]
# Use "datasets" for one figure per condition or "conditions" to overlay conditions from one file.
comparison = "datasets"
complete_lists_only = True
max_subjects = 0              # Zero includes all participants.
confidence_level = 0.95
plot_seed = 0

project_root = None
output_dir = "results/spc"
figure_dir = None             # Defaults to output_dir.
figure_str = "spc"            # An empty name displays figures without saving.

# Optional plot settings for parameterized runs.
color_cycle = None
contrast_name = None
ylim = (0, 1)
yticks = None

title: Serial position curves
text:
Load the responses
Relative paths use the project directory. The data guide describes the expected file format.


Install JAXCMR in Colab
import sys

if "google.colab" in sys.modules:
    %pip install --upgrade "jaxcmr @ git+https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git@main"




Import plotting and dataset operations
import re

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from jaxcmr.analyses.spc import plot_spc
from jaxcmr.dataset import select_conditions
from jaxcmr.examples import copy_example_inputs
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data, resolve_project_path, resolve_project_root
from jaxcmr.plotting import comparison_panels, save_figure




Load response files
root = resolve_project_root(project_root)
copy_example_inputs(data_paths, base_dir=root)
datasets = [load_data(resolve_project_path(path, root), max_subjects=max_subjects) for path in data_paths]

title: Serial position curves
text:
Check the selected trials
The counts show how many lists and participants contribute to each curve. Set trial_query to run one selection in place of the listed queries. Use selection_label to name it.


Select trials and report coverage
if trial_query is not None:
    trial_queries, labels = [trial_query], [selection_label]

masks_by_dataset = []
for name, dataset in zip(data_labels, datasets, strict=True):
    selections = select_conditions(dataset, trial_queries, complete_lists_only=complete_lists_only)
    masks_by_dataset.append([selection.mask for selection in selections])
    for label, selection in zip(labels, selections, strict=True):
        print(f"{name} / {label}: {selection.trial_count} lists, {selection.participant_count} participants")


Observed / Mixed: 246 lists, 123 participants
Observed / Pure emotional: 122 lists, 122 participants
Observed / Pure neutral: 123 lists, 123 participants

title: Serial position curves
text:
Recall by study position
Each point is the mean of the participants’ recall probabilities at that position. Error bars show bootstrap confidence intervals for that mean. If an item appeared more than once on a list, recalling it credits each of its study positions once.
When saving several figures, the notebook adds the condition number and label to each filename. A single figure uses figure_str alone.


Plot and save each comparison
panels = comparison_panels(
    datasets, masks_by_dataset, data_labels, labels, mode=comparison
)
for number, panel in enumerate(panels, start=1):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.2))
    plot_spc(panel["datasets"], panel["trial_masks"], axis=ax, labels=panel["labels"],
             color_cycle=color_cycle, confidence_level=confidence_level, bootstrap_seed=plot_seed)

    title = data_labels[0] if comparison == "conditions" else panel["title"]
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel("Study position", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel("Recall probability", fontsize=12)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=10)
    ax.set_ylim(ylim)
    if yticks is not None:
        ax.set_yticks(yticks)
    if len(panel["labels"]) > 1:
        ax.legend(title=contrast_name, frameon=False)

    if figure_str:
        suffix = None
        if len(panels) > 1:
            label = re.sub(r"\W+", "_", panel["title"].casefold()).strip("_")
            suffix = f"{number}_{label}".rstrip("_")
        save_figure(resolve_project_path(figure_dir or output_dir, root), figure_str,
                    suffix=suffix, figure=fig)
    else:
        fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)
